dishes.name: Baked Apple
dishes.serviceNote: Breakfast tasting ($80) includes tasting portions and all listed drinks. Tree nuts (pecans), dairy; oats may carry gluten, confirm.

kept.a: You never sell the Baked Apple alone: it comes with the Traditional Breakfast, so you sell the tasting. Offer the tasting to a first visit, a birthday or anyone who asks for the real Brennan's breakfast, and name the apple as the gentle first course. If a guest wants wine beyond the included drinks, the Dr. Hermann Auslese half-bottle at $80 is the match and lasts to dessert, once lineup confirms it is still offered. Say: “The tasting starts sweet and gentle: a warm baked apple with an oat and pecan crumble, like an apple crisp.”

kept.q: How is the baked apple made?
kept.a: A whole apple, peeled and cored, baked until soft under a crumble of rolled oats, pecans, raisins, brown sugar and cinnamon, then glazed with brown sugar and served with sweetened creme fraiche. Warm, soft and cinnamon sweet, a gentle start to the breakfast. The cellar dossier calls its Auslese pairing the best block in the book.

The Baked Apple is the first plated course of the Traditional Breakfast at Brennan's, our $80 tasting, and it is served only on that menu.

A whole apple is peeled, cored and baked until soft under a crumble of rolled oats, pecans, raisins, brown sugar and cinnamon, then glazed with brown sugar. It goes out with sweetened crème fraîche, a slightly tangy cultured cream, beside it.

What the guest gets is a warm, soft apple under its crumble and glaze, with the cool cream alongside. It eats like a warm apple crisp: tender fruit, a little crunch, cinnamon sweetness, and the tang of the cream to balance it.

Breakfast here has always been a long, celebratory meal, and this is its gentle start. It follows the Brandy Milk Punch eye opener and comes before the soup. The tasting includes its drinks, so wine is only ever an extra here; for a guest who wants one, the Dr. Hermann Auslese half-bottle tastes of baked apple and honey and carries on to the Bananas Foster.

Asked: Is it very sweet?

Answer: It is sweet like a warm apple crisp, and the sweetened crème fraîche beside it is slightly tangy, which balances it.

Asked: What is crème fraîche?

Answer: Krem FRESH: a slightly tangy cultured cream. On the apple it is sweetened; on the coffee cake it is whipped.

Asked: Does wine come with this course?

Answer: The tasting includes the Brandy Milk Punch before it and drinks with the later courses. Wine here is an extra: the Mosel Auslese half-bottle tastes of baked apple and honey.

The Baked Apple fires as the first plated course, after the Brandy Milk Punch and before the soup, so set the tasting's pace from the greeting. The tasting includes its drinks: offer wine only as an extra, never as part of the price. For a guest skipping the milk punch, the Café Glacé de la Maison is the zero-proof match. Take the filet temperature now, with the tasting order, not when the steak course fires. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

value.s45: Breakfast at Brennan’s has always been a long, celebratory meal, and the baked apple is a gentle start. The apple is baked until soft, with a crumble of oatmeal, pecans and raisins, then glazed with brown sugar. Sweetened crème fraîche, a slightly tangy cultured cream, balances the sweetness. It’s warm and comforting, and it comes after your Brandy Milk Punch eye opener, before the soup.

value.why: A brown-sugar glaze calls for a wine at least as sweet: the Auslese’s apple, apricot and honey mirror the fruit, and its acidity keeps a warm, sweet course fresh.
value.sayIt: The tasting includes its own drinks, but if you’d like wine, a half-bottle of Mosel Auslese tastes of baked apple and honey, and it carries you right through to the Bananas Foster.
value.whyThisWine: It’s a warm, sweet baked apple, so a sweet Riesling is the match. It’s honeyed but bright, like biting into a crisp apple, and it keeps the course light.
value.palate: Brown-sugar glaze makes a dry wine taste tart; the Auslese is sweeter than the glaze, so the apple tastes richer and the wine stays lush. Its acidity mirrors the apple’s own tartness and cuts the crème fraîche, while honey and apricot bridge to the raisins and caramel. Low alcohol keeps it gentle for the first course of breakfast.
value.secondWhy: A lighter glass of the Berres Riesling, taste it first: if it’s off-dry it works; if it’s dry, the glaze will make it taste tart.
value.serve: The Traditional Breakfast includes a Brandy Milk Punch here; offer wine only as an extra. The 375 ml half-bottle carries through to Bananas Foster, 2 to 3 oz pours in a small glass. The Dr. Hermann half-bottle is off the current glass page: confirm at lineup that it is still offered before leading with it.
value.avoid: Avoid dry sparkling and dry reds: the brown sugar makes them taste sour and thin.
value.zeroProofWhy: For guests skipping the milk punch, its cardamom-clove syrup echoes the baked-apple spice.

dishes.name: Petite Filet Mignon
dishes.serviceNote: Ask filet temperature when you take the tasting order, not when the course fires. Rösti is RUHSH-tee. Likely dairy (butter).

kept.a: The filet comes with the tasting, so the sale is the temperature and the pour. When you take the tasting order, ask how the guest likes the filet and write it on the ticket. For a guest who wants more than the included glass, the Inglenook Rubicon 2010 by the glass at $70 is the step up, aged and silky with cedar and tobacco; the Moulin d'Issan at $16 is a fuller glass. Say: “The last savory course is a petite filet with a crisp potato rösti, and we pour a juicy Côtes du Rhône with it.”

The Petite Filet Mignon is the fourth course of the Traditional Breakfast, the last savory course before the Bananas Foster, and the steak a grand New Orleans breakfast has always included.

It is a small filet mignon, the most tender cut of beef, cooked to the temperature the guest chose when the tasting was ordered. Beside it sit a potato rösti, RUHSH-tee, a Swiss-style cake of shredded potato fried golden and crisp, and garlicky wilted spinach.

The plate is simple on purpose: the beef, the crisp potato cake and the green spinach. It tastes tender, beefy and clean, with crunch from the rösti and garlic from the spinach.

The course comes with a 4 oz glass of Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’, a Côtes du Rhône from old vine Syrah grown beside Châteauneuf-du-Pape: black raspberry, pepper and soft tannins, juicy enough for red meat and light enough for the morning. The pour is included in the $80 price.

Asked: How will the filet be cooked?

Answer: To the temperature you choose now. We take it with the tasting order so the kitchen has it right when the course fires.

Asked: What is a rösti?

Answer: RUHSH-tee: a Swiss-style cake of shredded potato, fried golden and crisp.

Asked: What is the red wine?

Answer: Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’, a Côtes du Rhône from old vine Syrah, juicy and soft with a little pepper. The menu prints the 2023, and I read the label before naming it.

kept.q: What do we pour with the filet, and what is it?
kept.a: With the filet we pour Domaine de Chateaumar 'Cuvee Vincent', a Cotes du Rhone from the Southern Rhone made from old vine Syrah: black raspberry, black pepper, soft tannins, juicy and just right for red meat at breakfast. The tasting menu prints 2023; read the label before naming it.

Ask the filet temperature when you take the tasting order, not when the course fires. The Côtes du Rhône is an included 4 oz pour as the course fires: never double-pour, and read the label before you name the 2023 the menu prints. By this course the table has had a milk punch, a Bloody Bull and Champagne, so offer the Personality, our spirit-free sparkling rosé, in place of the red without being asked; the tasting price does not change. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Louisiana BBQ Lobster
dishes.serviceNote: Shellfish (lobster), pork (’nduja), dairy (butter). Moderate heat. Confirm the kitchen’s BBQ sauce at lineup. Dinner tasting: $80, wine pairing $120 (4 oz pours).

kept.a: The lobster sells the dinner tasting and the pairing together. Offer the tasting to a celebration, a first visit or a table that wants to see the kitchen's range, and offer the $120 pairing with it: this is the course where a round white Burgundy earns its place. Ask about spice early; for a guest who is wary of heat, the Berres Riesling at $14 is the gentler glass. Say: “Our second course is lobster in the New Orleans barbecue style, buttery and peppery, over white beans with a little spicy ’nduja.”

The Louisiana BBQ Lobster is the second course of our $80 dinner tasting, between the Grand Isle Jewel oysters and the Redfish Véronique.

New Orleans barbecue is not a smoker or a tomato sauce. It is the buttery, peppery style made famous by barbecue shrimp, and here the kitchen gives that treatment to lobster. The lobster sits on a white bean stew with ’nduja, en-DOO-yah, a soft, spreadable, spicy pork sausage from Calabria in southern Italy that melts into the beans.

The guest gets sweet lobster over a creamy stew of beans warmed by the sausage. It tastes sweet and rich from the lobster and the butter, with a warm red-pepper heat and a smoky, creamy base.

It is the course that brings spice into the tasting. On the $120 wine pairing it is poured with a 4 oz glass of white Burgundy, the Fichet ‘Château London’ Mâcon-Igé 2024, as the guide and the current menu print: Chardonnay round enough for the butter and fresh enough for the ’nduja.

Asked: Is it barbecue like a smoker?

Answer: No. New Orleans barbecue means a buttery, peppery sauce, the style made famous by barbecue shrimp, not smoke or tomato.

Asked: Is it spicy?

Answer: The ’nduja gives the beans a warm red-pepper heat. How hot it runs tonight is a lineup question for the chef, so I will check with the kitchen before promising mild.

Asked: What is ’nduja?

Answer: En-DOO-yah: a soft, spreadable spicy pork sausage from Calabria, in southern Italy, that melts into the beans.

Two things on this course are settled at lineup. The white is the Fichet Mâcon-Igé 2024 the guide and the current menu print; read the supplement card before you name it. And ask the chef what is in the BBQ sauce and how much heat the ’nduja carries tonight. Pour the 4 oz just before the course lands. If the spice runs hot, the Berres Riesling is the lighter, sweeter swap. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.q: Which white is poured with the lobster tonight?
kept.a: With the lobster we pour a white Burgundy, Chardonnay with body for the lobster and butter and a fresh finish against the spicy nduja. The guide and the current menu both print the Fichet Château London Mâcon-Igé 2024; check the supplement card all the same. By the heat rule the Berres Riesling is the sharper tool for the nduja: if it runs hot, the Berres is lighter and a touch sweeter, and we can swap it.

dishes.name: Roasted Rohan Duck Breast
dishes.serviceNote: Duck is usually served medium-rare to medium, confirm the kitchen’s standard and mention it. Tree nuts (hazelnuts). Dinner tasting course four.

kept.a: Sell the duck as the heart of the dinner tasting and the reason to take the pairing. Guests who love duck, red wine or a classic French plate lean in here. Name the Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet with it; for a guest who prefers Pinot Noir, the Damien Martin Bourgogne at $18 is the classic lighter match. Read tonight's garnish from the kitchen before you describe it. Say: “Our fourth course is roasted Rohan duck, rich and rosy, and the pairing pours a Coombsville Cabernet with it.”

The Roasted Rohan Duck Breast is the fourth course of our $80 dinner tasting, the last savory course before The Snickers.

Rohan, ROH-han, is a special cross bred for the D'Artagnan company and raised in New York's Hudson Valley for tender, rosy meat. The breast is roasted so the skin renders and the meat stays rosy. On the guide's card and the current menu it comes with peaches glazed in cane syrup, Louisiana's own sugarcane syrup, lighter and more buttery than molasses, and candied hazelnuts.

The guest gets slices of rosy duck with caramel-glazed fruit and a little crunch from the nuts. It tastes rich and savory against the sweet fruit.

Duck and fruit is a French classic, and this is the Louisiana version. On the $120 pairing it is poured with a 4 oz glass of Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet Sauvignon 2021, dark fruit for the peaches and structure for the duck.

The current menu prints the plate as the guide does; the garnish is still confirmed with the kitchen each night.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: A young Napa Cabernet against cane syrup peaches is a real tension and the guide admits it. From the list the Durban is the better technical red: ripe fruit, round tannin, body for the fat. The guide's avoid line excludes tart light reds while its second choice is a light Bourgogne; a ripe 2023 Bourgogne is not tart, which is why it stands.

Asked: What is Rohan duck?

Answer: A special cross bred for the D'Artagnan company and raised in New York's Hudson Valley for tender, rosy meat.

Asked: How is it cooked?

Answer: Roasted so the skin renders and the meat stays rosy. The kitchen's standard temperature is a lineup question, and I confirm it before the course.

Asked: Can I have Pinot Noir instead of the Cabernet?

Answer: The Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir is on our glass list at $18, and Pinot Noir with duck is the classic lighter match. I will ask a manager whether it can replace the pairing pour.

The guide and the current menu both print cane syrup glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts; confirm tonight's plate with the kitchen before you describe it. Ask the chef the temperature the duck is served at and mention it. Open the Cabernet 30 to 60 minutes ahead and pour it at 60 to 64°F in a Bordeaux glass. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Blackberry Trifle
dishes.serviceNote: Coconut; eggs and dairy (curds); gluten and likely almonds (financiers are traditionally made with almond flour, confirm). Chia has a seedy texture, mention it for guests who dislike that. Sweet: suggest it to share.

kept.a: Suggest the trifle when a table settles in and is reading the egg dishes: it is a sweet starter to share, not a dessert to save. It suits a guest who wants something light and fruity, or a table celebrating with a long breakfast. With it, the Personality at $16 keeps things light, and the Auslese half-bottle at $80, if lineup says it is still on the list, carries on to the Bananas Foster. Say: “While you look at the eggs, our Blackberry Trifle is a lovely one to share: bright, tart and creamy.”

The Blackberry Trifle is one of the three sweet starters on our breakfast and lunch menu, at $14, and a lighter way to begin the meal.

A trifle is a layered dessert. Ours layers blackberry curd and lemon curd with coconut chia pudding, chia seeds soaked until they turn soft and spoonable, and finishes with blackberry financier biscuits, fee-nahn-SYAY, small, buttery French cakes, traditionally made with almond flour, that give it texture; what is in ours is a question for the kitchen and the service note.

What arrives is a layered sweet of two curds, the pudding and the little cakes. It tastes bright, tart and creamy, fruity more than sugary, so it wakes the palate up rather than weighing it down.

It is made to share: it belongs in the middle of the table while the guests look over the egg dishes. If the table wants wine with its sweet starters, the Dr. Hermann Auslese half-bottle is the match, honeyed and racy enough for the curds, and it lasts through to dessert. Without alcohol, the Personality, a zero-proof sparkling rosé, keeps it light.

Asked: Is it a dessert?

Answer: It is listed as a starter, one of three sweet ones, and it is made to share before the eggs. It is tart and fruity more than sugary.

Asked: What is a financier?

Answer: Fee-nahn-SYAY: a small, buttery French cake, traditionally made with almond flour. Ours are blackberry; what goes into them is a question I take to the kitchen.

Asked: What is chia pudding?

dishes.name: Framboise French Toast
dishes.serviceNote: Gluten, eggs, dairy (brioche, custard, mascarpone). Listed as a starter, upsell it for the table to share. Pronounce framboise frahm-BWAHZ.

It is listed with the starters, so suggest it for the table. Say: “Framboise is French for raspberry: our own citrus brioche as French toast, with mascarpone mousse and fresh raspberries.”

The Framboise French Toast is a sweet starter on our breakfast and lunch menu at $16, made to share or to enjoy as a sweet course.

Framboise, frahm-BWAHZ, is French for raspberry, and raspberry is the star. We bake our own citrus brioche, a rich, buttery egg bread, and turn it into French toast. It is finished with mascarpone mousse, a rich Italian cream cheese whipped light, a raspberry coulis, which is a smooth fruit sauce, and fresh local raspberries on top.

The guest gets French toast under the mousse, the red coulis and whole berries. It tastes rich, soft and custardy, with bright, tart berry against the cream and a little citrus from the brioche.

Baking the brioche in house is what sets it apart. With it, the Dr. Hermann Auslese half-bottle keeps the raspberries juicy, and our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory balances the sweetness for a guest who wants no wine.

Asked: How do you say it, and what does it mean?

Answer: Frahm-BWAHZ. It is French for raspberry.

Asked: Is the brioche made here?

Answer: Yes. We bake our own citrus brioche, a rich, buttery egg bread, and make the French toast from it.

Asked: What is mascarpone?

Answer: Mahs-kar-POH-neh: a rich Italian cream cheese. Here it is whipped into a light mousse.

It sits on the starter list, so a guest may not expect a sweet plate: say sweet when you describe it, and suggest sharing. Steer away from Brut sparkling and dry rosé, however festive: the coulis and the mousse leave them tart and hard. If a guest wants wine, pour the Auslese 2 to 3 oz in a small white glass as the plate lands. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Café Brûlot Coffee Cake
dishes.serviceNote: Tree nuts (pecans), gluten, eggs, dairy. Contains coffee (caffeine). Brûlot is broo-LOH. Suggest it to share or as a sweet course with coffee.

kept.a: Suggest it to share at the start, or as the sweet course with coffee at the end. It suits a coffee lover, and a guest who likes chocolate but not a heavy dessert. The easy pairing is a cup of our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory at $11, or the Café Glacé de la Maison when they want it cold. Say: “It is named for café brûlot, our famous spiced coffee: a chicory coffee and dark chocolate cake with a spiced citrus glaze.”

The Café Brûlot Coffee Cake is a sweet starter on our breakfast and lunch menu at $14. It is named for café brûlot, ka-FAY broo-LOH, the classic New Orleans coffee flamed with brandy, orange and lemon peel, cinnamon and clove.

The cake borrows those flavors. It is a chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake with pecans for crunch, finished with a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche, a slightly tangy cultured cream that keeps it from being too sweet.

The guest gets a dark, moist cake with its glaze and a spoon of the cream. It tastes roasty and chocolatey, with orange and warm spice.

Café brûlot itself is on no current menu as a drink: this cake is the only Brûlot item, and only two desserts are flamed at the table. The natural partner is a cup of our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory. For wine, Banyuls, a sweet red from the south of France, carries its own cocoa and coffee notes, once the sommelier confirms it can be poured at breakfast.

Asked: Can I order a café brûlot to drink?

Answer: Not from today's menus. The cake is the only Brûlot item, and only two desserts are flamed at the table, so I do not offer the drink until the house confirms it.

Asked: Is there coffee in the cake?

Answer: Yes: chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate, so it carries caffeine.

Asked: What wine goes with it?

Answer: Banyuls, a sweet red from the south of France with cocoa and coffee notes, if the sommelier confirms it can be poured at breakfast; otherwise our coffee with chicory.

Never offer café brûlot as a drink: it is on no current menu, and a guest who hears the name may ask for the flamed coffee. The Banyuls is the dinner tasting's dessert pour, so confirm with the sommelier that it can be poured at breakfast, and at what price, before you offer it. Avoid dry reds and Brut Champagne with the cake: chocolate and coffee turn them bitter and sour. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Louisiana Oysters
dishes.serviceNote: Shellfish (oysters), dairy (butter), gluten (saltines). Worcestershire traditionally contains anchovy (fish). Peppery, not hot. Confirm at lineup how the oysters are cooked and plated, and how many come per order.

kept.a: Offer the oysters to a table that wants something savory to share before the eggs, or to a guest who asks for a real New Orleans flavor. Explain the barbecue straight away so nobody expects smoke. Pour the Gainey Chardonnay at $17 with it; the Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin is the step up, and the Oh! What It Seemed to Be, lemon and fig, is the zero-proof match. Say: “Our Louisiana Oysters come in New Orleans barbecue sauce, which here means buttery and peppery, with pickled collards and a saltine crunch.”

The Louisiana Oysters are a starter on our breakfast and lunch menu at $19, and the oyster dish of the daytime menu.

In New Orleans, barbecue does not mean a smoker or a tomato sauce. It means the style made famous by barbecue shrimp: a rich, buttery sauce with plenty of black pepper. The kitchen serves Louisiana oysters in that sauce, then adds pickled collard greens for a sharp, bright bite, shallots, and a fried saltine crumble for crunch.

The guest gets oysters in a peppery butter sauce, with the bright greens and a crunchy crumble. It tastes rich and peppery, with a sharp pickled bite: peppery, not hot.

It is a dish to share before the eggs, and a real New Orleans flavor. The guide pours the Gainey Estate Chardonnay with it, creamy enough for the butter sauce and fresh enough for the pickled greens; for a guest who wants bubbles cutting the butter, the house Champagne is the second choice.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Gainey first and Leflaive as the step up is the right order here, as the guide prints it: the butter sauce wants a creamy Chardonnay, and lean, green whites make butter taste flat.

Asked: Is it smoky, or a tomato barbecue sauce?

Answer: Neither. New Orleans barbecue is a buttery, peppery sauce, the style made famous by barbecue shrimp.

Asked: Is it hot?

Answer: Peppery, not hot. The pickled collards add a sharp, bright bite.

Asked: How many oysters come in an order, and are they cooked?

Answer: They come in the warm sauce. The count per order and how the kitchen cooks and plates them are on tonight's lineup list, so I will check with the kitchen before I say a number.

Do not confuse these with the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters: the Louisiana Oysters are the daytime starter, $19, in the buttery BBQ sauce; the Grand Isle Jewels are the dinner starter, $22, raw with a mignonette. Ask the chef at lineup what is in the sauce, how the oysters are cooked and plated, and how many come per order. Pour the Gainey around 50°F so its creamy texture shows. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Creole Tomato Tostada
dishes.serviceNote: No meat listed, confirm with the kitchen for vegetarians. Dairy (burrata). Ask about gluten in the okra tostada. Seasonal: Creole tomatoes are a summer crop, so expect it to change as the season turns.

kept.a: Suggest the tostada as a light first course on a warm evening, to a guest who likes fresh, seasonal plates or wants something before a rich entrée. Tell them the tomatoes are the season's, and it will not be on the menu for long. Pour the Minuty rosé at $17 with it; the Durand Sauvignon Blanc at $14 is the crisp alternative, and the Personality, a zero-proof sparkling rosé, the spirit-free one. Say: “While the Creole tomatoes are in season, the tostada is a lovely light start: tomatoes, creamy burrata and a crisp okra shell.”

The Creole Tomato Tostada is a dinner starter at $18, and our celebration of Louisiana tomato season.

Creole tomatoes are Louisiana's summer tomato: juicy, sweet and a little tart. Here they are mixed with heirloom tomatoes and served raw and simply, with creamy burrata, boo-RAH-tah, fresh mozzarella with a soft, creamy center. They sit on a crisp tostada, a flat shell the kitchen makes in house with okra, and a smoked tomato water, a clear, intensely tomatoey broth, is poured around.

The guest sees bright tomatoes and white burrata on the crisp shell, with the clear broth around them. It tastes juicy, sweet and tart, cool and creamy, with crunch and a whisper of smoke.

It is light, seasonal and gone when the tomatoes are, so it changes as the season turns. The Minuty rosé from Provence is the pour, dry and bright enough for raw tomato and delicate enough for the burrata.

Asked: What is burrata?

Answer: Boo-RAH-tah: fresh mozzarella with a soft, creamy center, cool and rich against the tomatoes.

Asked: What is smoked tomato water?

Answer: A clear, intensely tomatoey broth with a whisper of smoke, poured around the plate.

dishes.name: Louisiana Crab Claws
dishes.serviceNote: Shellfish (crab), dairy (butter). Finger food, bring napkins and a plate for shells per house standard. Fines herbes is feen ZAIRB.

kept.q: How do I describe the claws so nobody expects a cold cocktail claw?
kept.a: Our crab claws come warm, dressed in a brown butter vinaigrette, and you eat the meat straight off the claw. Say warm and off the claw when you describe them; use the pincer as a handle, bite and slide the cartilage out.

Suggest the claws to a table that wants something to share and pick at, or to a guest who loves crab. Say warm and off the claw, so nobody expects a cold cocktail claw. Pour the Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé at $40 by Coravin with it; for a leaner glass, the Durand Sauvignon Blanc at $14, and for no alcohol, the Oh! What It Seemed to Be. Say: “Our crab claws come warm in a brown butter vinaigrette with fines herbes: sweet crab, nutty butter, eaten right off the claw.”

The Louisiana Crab Claws are a dinner starter at $22, a Louisiana favorite and a dish to share.

Crab claws are sweet, delicate crab meat you eat straight off the claw, using the pincer as a handle. Ours come warm, dressed in a brown butter vinaigrette: butter cooked until it turns nutty and toasty, balanced with acidity so it is rich but bright. Fines herbes, feen ZAIRB, the classic French mix of parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, finish it with a soft, fresh green note.

The guest gets warm claws glossed in the vinaigrette under green herbs, with a plate for the shells and napkins brought at the same time. It tastes of sweet crab, nutty butter, bright acid and soft herbs.

It is simple and elegant. The guide pours the Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin with it, because white Burgundy's nutty richness mirrors the brown butter; the sommelier may suggest the Gainey Chardonnay as a lower priced, creamy option once it is confirmed to taste fresh.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: With the crab claws the Leflaive Macon is the pour: its nutty richness mirrors the brown butter and its acidity meets the vinaigrette. For a guest who wants something leaner, the Durand Loire Sauvignon Blanc works because the dressing is a vinaigrette, so its acid has something to meet; that is not true of the BBQ butter on the oysters. For bubbles, the house Extra Brut or Rare. The Gainey Chardonnay is the lower priced creamy option, not a change of style; the dossier would lead with the Gainey and keep the Leflaive as the step up on both crab dishes once the Gainey is confirmed to read fresh rather than oaky.

Asked: Are they cold, like a cocktail claw?

Answer: No, they come warm, dressed in a brown butter vinaigrette, and you eat the meat straight off the claw.

Asked: How do I eat them?

Answer: Hold the pincer as a handle, bite, and slide the cartilage out. I will bring a plate for the shells and extra napkins.

dishes.serviceNote: Raw shellfish: give the consumer advisory: raw oysters carry risk, especially for guests who are pregnant, immunocompromised or have liver disease. Fresno chili is mild. Know the count per order. On the dinner tasting they’re paired with Charles Lafitte Brut.

Fresno is a red Californian chili from the 1950s, about the heat of a jalapeno but fruitier and thinner walled; preserved and stirred into the mignonette it gives a gentle warmth, not real heat.

The Grand Isle Jewel Oysters are a dinner starter at $22, and the first course of our $80 dinner tasting.

Grand Isle is a barrier island on Louisiana's coast. Grand Isle Jewels are farmed oysters raised there in floating cages above the seabed and tumbled, so they grow a deep cup and a clean shell. The brand brought the island's farmers together in 2025 and honors the late Jules Melancon, the first permitted to farm off bottom there, in 2012. We serve them raw on the half shell with a mignonette, meen-yo-NET, the classic raw bar sauce of vinegar, shallot and cracked pepper, made here with preserved Fresno chili, and parsley.

The guest gets cold oysters on the shell with the mignonette and a green note of parsley. They taste clean, briny and cold, the vinegar bright and the chili a gentle warmth, not real heat.

Oysters and Champagne are the classic: the house Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut is the pour à la carte, and the dinner tasting pours Charles Lafitte Brut.

dishes.name: Steak Tartare Cannoli
dishes.serviceNote: Raw beef and cured egg yolk, consumer advisory. Dairy (crème fraîche). Ask about gluten and the fryer for the potato shell. Handheld; suggest eating it in a couple of bites. Bottarga is boh-TAR-gah.

kept.a: Suggest the cannoli to adventurous eaters, to a guest who loves steak tartare, and as a quick, fun bite while the table decides. The Steak Tartare Cannoli is a dinner starter at $17, a playful take on steak tartare.

Tartare is raw beef, finely chopped and seasoned. Instead of serving it with toast, the kitchen pipes it into a crisp potato shell shaped like a cannoli. Crème fraîche, krem FRESH, a tangy cultured cream, keeps it cool and silky, and an egg yolk cured until firm is grated over the top the way Italians grate bottarga, boh-TAR-gah, the cured fish roe, for a rich, salty finish.

The guest gets a handheld piece, two or three bites, crisp outside and cool within. It tastes cool, silky and savory, the shell crunching against the soft beef and the salty yolk.

It is the only dish on the current menus with the cured egg yolk, and a fun way to start dinner. The Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d'Alsace is the pour: all Pinot Noir, with red fruit for the raw beef and bubbles for the fried shell and the cream.

Answer: An egg yolk cured until firm and grated over the top, the way Italians grate bottarga, cured fish roe, for a rich, salty finish.

Answer: It is handheld: two or three bites.

dishes.name: Turtle Soup
dishes.serviceNote: Contains alcohol (Sherry), flag it for guests avoiding alcohol. Egg; dairy (brown butter). Creole turtle soups are usually roux-thickened, so ask the kitchen about gluten. On the breakfast tasting, guests choose this or the gumbo (served with a Bloody Bull). Say “turtle” plainly, many guests are trying it for the first time.

kept.a: Offer the turtle soup to every first visit, and to anyone who asks what New Orleans tastes like: it is the classic, at breakfast and at dinner. A cup before the eggs or the redfish sets the meal. Pour the house Champagne with it, $30 a glass on the current menu; Rare by the glass is the celebration step up, and the Café Glacé de la Maison is the zero-proof match. Say: “Our Turtle Soup is the Brennan's classic: all turtle, rich and savory, finished with a splash of aged Sherry.”

Turtle Soup is a Brennan's signature, $13 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and the soup on the Traditional Breakfast.

It is one of the great Creole soups, rich and long-cooked. Ours is made with 100% turtle meat, farm raised Louisiana freshwater turtle, never wild. Many New Orleans turtle soups stretch the turtle with veal and beef; ours is all turtle, with nothing padding it out. It is finished with brown butter spinach, grated egg and a splash of aged Sherry at the end.

The guest gets a deep, dark bowl with the spinach and egg through it. It tastes savory and meaty, with a toasty, earthy note from the brown butter spinach, richness from the egg, and a nutty, dry lift from the Sherry that cuts the richness. If they have never had turtle, it is like a rich, finely chopped stew.

It is the one bowl that tells a guest what Brennan's is about. Our house Champagne, very dry, cleans the palate between spoonfuls and picks up the Sherry.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Our house Champagne is Piper-Heidsieck's Extra Brut: very dry, with brioche and toasted nut from its time on the lees that pick up the Sherry while the bubbles clear the richness. For a step up, Rare is seventy percent Chardonnay with grilled almond and candied orange that meet the Sherry even more closely. Neither wine is oxidative; the Sherry echo is a fair secondary point behind dryness and bubbles.

Asked: Is it real turtle?

Answer: Yes: 100% turtle meat, farm raised Louisiana freshwater turtle, never wild. Many turtle soups stretch it with veal and beef; ours is all turtle.

Asked: Is it the turtles in the courtyard?

Answer: No. The courtyard turtles are pets, named for sauces; the soup is not the turtles.

Asked: Is there alcohol in it?

Answer: Yes, a splash of aged Sherry finishes it. Whether it goes in in the kitchen or at the table is a lineup question, so I will check with the kitchen for anyone avoiding alcohol.

Say turtle plainly: many guests are trying it for the first time. It carries aged Sherry, so flag it for anyone avoiding alcohol. On the Traditional Breakfast the guest chooses this or the gumbo, poured with a Bloody Bull. Do not confuse it with the Seafood Gumbo, the other $13 soup. Never name the turtle supplier until the kitchen confirms it at lineup. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.q: Does the dining room gumbo follow the published recipe?
kept.a: Our published gumbo recipe starts with a dark mahogany roux, andouille and okra in crab stock, and the shrimp, crab and oysters go in at the very end so they stay tender; the published recipe carries okra, tomato and file, which the menu does not list, so say published recipe, never menu. Suggest the gumbo to a guest who wants something hearty before an egg dish, to seafood lovers, and to anyone choosing a soup on the Traditional Breakfast. What It Seemed to Be. Say: “Our Seafood Gumbo is shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille, over Louisiana popcorn rice: the taste of Louisiana in a bowl.”

The Seafood Gumbo is a Brennan's signature, $13 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and the other soup choice on the Traditional Breakfast.

Gumbo, GUM-boh, is the dish that says Louisiana: a stew built on a dark roux. Ours is all about the seafood, shrimp, crab and oysters, so every spoonful has sweetness and a little brine. Andouille, ahn-DOO-ee, a coarse, smoked pork sausage, gives it a savory, smoky backbone and a gentle warmth. It is served over popcorn rice, a Louisiana long-grain with a nutty, toasty aroma that really does smell a little like popcorn.

The guest gets a hearty bowl of seafood and sausage over the rice. It tastes savory, briny and smoky, with mild to moderate spice.

Our published gumbo recipe starts with a dark mahogany roux, and the seafood goes in at the very end so it stays tender; whether the dining room follows it is confirmed at lineup. The Berres Riesling is the pour: light and bright, it cools the spice and keeps the seafood sweet.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: With the seafood gumbo I reach for the Berres Riesling: low alcohol, no tannin and a touch of sweetness, so it cools the andouille's spice and keeps the shrimp, crab and oysters tasting sweet. If the guest wants red, the Bourgogne Pinot Noir is light enough for the smoky sausage; it is the alternative, not the first choice.

Asked: Is it spicy?

Answer: Mild to moderate. The andouille gives it a gentle warmth, and a light Riesling calms it.

Asked: What is popcorn rice?

Answer: A Louisiana long-grain rice with a nutty, toasty aroma that smells a little like popcorn.

Asked: Is there okra or filé in it?

Answer: The menu lists shrimp, crab, oysters, andouille and popcorn rice. Our published recipe carries okra, tomato and filé, but whether tonight's gumbo follows it is a lineup question, so I will check with the kitchen.

Do not confuse it with the Turtle Soup: both are $13, and the breakfast tasting offers either. Say published recipe, never menu, when you mention okra, tomato or filé, and only once the chef confirms the dining room follows it. Taste the open Berres at lineup so you can say honestly whether it is dry or off-dry, and keep it well chilled: heat reads hotter with warm wine. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Say: “Our Creole Caesar is crisp gem lettuce in a smoked oyster dressing, with Grana Padano and crisps made from Leidenheimer bread.”

The Creole Caesar is our salad, $15 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and our Louisiana take on a Caesar.

It starts with gem lettuce, small, sweet and very crisp, so it holds up to a creamy dressing. The dressing is made with smoked oysters, which give it the deep, savory flavor a Caesar is known for, with a smoky edge. Grana Padano, GRAH-nah pah-DAH-noh, a hard, nutty Italian cheese like Parmesan, adds salt and richness, and the crisps are made from Leidenheimer, LY-den-hy-mer, the bakery behind New Orleans' po-boy bread since 1896.

The guest gets crisp leaves in a creamy dressing with shaved cheese and crunchy bread crisps. It tastes crisp, creamy, smoky and savory.

It is a lighter start before an egg dish or the redfish, and it appears at both meals. The Pazo das Bruxas Albariño is the pour: citrusy, with a salty, coastal edge that meets the smoked oyster dressing.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?

Answer: That is a question for the kitchen, and it is on the lineup list; I will check with the kitchen before I answer.

Asked: What is Grana Padano?

Answer: A hard, nutty Italian cheese, much like Parmesan.

Always mention the smoked oyster dressing when you describe the Caesar: guests do not expect oysters in a Caesar. Whether the dressing also holds raw egg or anchovy, and whether the oysters are smoked in house, are lineup questions for the chef. Pour the Albariño well chilled as the salad fires, and say the smoked oyster dressing again as you pour. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.serviceNote: Eggs (soft poached yolks, and in the hollandaise), dairy, gluten, pork; the marchand de vin is made with red wine. Check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs. Hussarde is hoo-SARD. On the breakfast tasting it comes with a 4 oz pour of Charles Lafitte Brut.

kept.a: Lead every first breakfast with the Hussarde: it is the egg dish we are known for, and the third course of the Traditional Breakfast. Offer it to anyone who loves Eggs Benedict. Pour the house Champagne, $30 on the current menu; for a celebration, Rare by the glass at $75; for a guest who wants red, the Damien Martin Bourgogne at $18, which meets the red wine sauce. Say: “If it's your first breakfast with us, Eggs Hussarde is the one: our own English muffins, coffee-cured bacon and two sauces.”

Eggs Hussarde, hoo-SARD, is our signature egg dish, $27 at breakfast and lunch, and the heart of the Traditional Breakfast.

It is the New Orleans cousin of Eggs Benedict. We make our own English muffins, and the Canadian bacon is cured with coffee, so it is smoky and a little roasty. On top go poached eggs and two sauces: hollandaise, the buttery, lemony egg-yolk sauce, and marchand de vin, mar-SHAHN duh VAN, the wine merchant's sauce, a savory red wine and mushroom sauce.

The guest gets the eggs on their muffins and bacon, the two sauces side by side. It tastes rich, buttery and savory, with a deep, winey note and a bright, lemony edge.

Paul Blangé, the house's first chef, is credited with creating it, alongside Bananas Foster and Chicken Pontalba; confirm the house's wording before telling that story. Eggs and Champagne are made for each other: our house Piper-Heidsieck is very dry, so it keeps the hollandaise feeling light.

Asked: How is it different from Eggs Benedict?

Answer: It has two sauces: hollandaise and marchand de vin, a savory red wine and mushroom sauce. And we make the English muffins and cure the Canadian bacon with coffee.

Asked: Was it invented here?

Answer: Our first chef, Paul Blangé, is credited with it. I use the house's own wording once a manager confirms it.

Asked: Can I have the eggs firmer?

Answer: The poached yolks are soft. I will check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs.

Do not confuse it with Eggs Owen, the heartier $32 plate with short rib débris and the same two sauces. The tasting pour is Charles Lafitte Brut, 4 oz, as the guide and the current menu print; confirm the bottle at lineup and never double-pour. Ask the chef how tonight's marchand de vin is built, and the manager whether to say created here and how to say Hussarde. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Eggs Sardou
dishes.serviceNote: No meat listed, confirm the creamed spinach and sauce with the kitchen for strict vegetarians. Eggs, dairy (Parmesan, cream, butter). Crispy artichokes are likely breaded or fried, ask about gluten. Sardou is sar-DOO.

It is a lovely contrast to a Hussarde across the table. Pour the Durand Sauvignon Blanc at $14, crisp and herbal; for a celebrating table, the Pierre Sparr rosé at $18; without alcohol, the Oh! What It Seemed to Be. Say: “Eggs Sardou is a New Orleans classic: poached eggs over crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach, with a tangy tomato béarnaise.”

Eggs Sardou, sar-DOO, is one of the classic New Orleans egg dishes, a Brennan's signature at $26 on the breakfast and lunch menu.

It was created at Antoine's, usually dated 1908, for the French playwright Victorien Sardou. The original set poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with hollandaise, anchovy, ham and truffle, with no spinach; the creamed spinach most kitchens use came later. Ours fries the artichokes until crisp, makes the creamed spinach with Parmesan, and swaps the hollandaise for Choron, sho-ROHN, a béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, with tomato folded in.

The guest gets poached eggs over the crispy artichokes and creamy spinach, finished with the Choron. It tastes creamy and rich, with crunch, and the tomato and tarragon keep it tangy and herbal.

It is our version of a classic born down the street, never a Brennan's invention. Artichokes are hard on most wines, and a crisp Loire Sauvignon Blanc is the exception, so the Durand is the pour.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Confirmed: the artichoke exception. Artichokes are hard on most wines and Loire Sauvignon Blanc loves them.

Asked: Was it created here?

Answer: No: it was created at Antoine's, usually dated 1908, for the playwright Victorien Sardou. Ours is the creamed spinach version, with crispy artichokes and Choron sauce.

Asked: What is Choron?

Answer: Sho-ROHN: a béarnaise, butter, egg yolk, shallot and tarragon, with tomato folded in, so it is tangy and herbal.

Asked: Are the artichokes fried?

Answer: They come crispy; whether they are breaded is a lineup question, and I will check with the kitchen before I answer.

Never present Eggs Sardou as a Brennan's invention: it was born at Antoine's. A guest asking whether it holds meat, or whether it suits a diet, goes to the kitchen: the creamed spinach and the sauce are confirmed there, not from memory. Ask the chef whether the artichokes are breaded as the published recipe has them. Avoid oaky Chardonnay and tannic reds with artichoke. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Owen Brennan opened the restaurant in 1946 and died in 1955. Do not say Eggs Owen is named for him unless a manager confirms it; the menu does not say. Eggs Owen today is short rib braised in red wine until it falls apart, over a Creole spiced potato, with a soft boiled egg and the same two sauces as the Hussarde. Eggs Owen is our heartiest egg dish, $32 on the breakfast and lunch menu, and steak and eggs, New Orleans style.

It is built on short rib débris. Débris, DAY-bree, is the New Orleans word for slow-cooked meat that falls apart into its own gravy; Mother's on Poydras Street, open since 1938, made the word famous. Ours is short rib braised in red wine until it falls apart. It sits with a Creole-spiced potato and a soft-boiled egg, so the yolk runs into everything, and it takes the same two sauces as the Hussarde: hollandaise for richness, and marchand de vin, a savory red wine and mushroom sauce that doubles down on the braise.

The guest gets a generous plate of tender beef, potato and egg under the two sauces. It tastes meaty, rich and saucy, with mild spice and silky yolk.

Both sauces carry red wine, so a red makes sense: the Domaine de Durban from the Southern Rhône is ripe and generous, with soft tannins gentle enough for the eggs.

The duck is a Rohan duck leg made as confit, kohn-FEE: cured and cooked slowly in its own fat until it is tender, with crisp skin. Sweet, savory, rich, it’s a showstopper for a brunch guest who wants something different.

value.why: Riesling’s acidity cuts the duck fat and foie gras butter, and its ripe fruit meets the maple syrup.
value.sayIt: With the duck and maple, the Berres Riesling is lovely, bright acidity for the richness, ripe fruit for the syrup.
value.whyThisWine: It’s rich duck with maple syrup, so I want brightness and a touch of fruit. This German Riesling cuts the richness and loves the maple, it keeps every bite fresh.
value.palate: Confit fat and foie gras butter coat the palate; Riesling’s high acidity cuts straight through and refreshes. Maple syrup would make a dry, tannic red taste thin and bitter, but the Riesling’s ripe stone fruit keeps pace with the sweetness, and the mustard’s tang is echoed by the wine’s acidity. The result is sweet-savory balance: rich duck, bright wine, and syrup that tastes fruity rather than cloying.
value.secondWhy: Pinot Noir and duck is a classic, for a guest who wants red.
value.serve: The Berres is off-dry, so lead with it; taste the open bottle at lineup if the vintage has changed. Well chilled, white-wine glass, poured as the dish fires.
value.avoid: Avoid tannic Cabernet and Bordeaux: maple sweetness makes tannin taste harsh and strips the fruit.
value.zeroProofWhy: chicory cold brew with cardamom-clove syrup echoes the maple and cuts the fat with roast.

dishes.name: New Orleans Shrimp & Grits
dishes.serviceNote: Shellfish (shrimp), pork (tasso), dairy (pimento cheese), likely gluten (fried coatings). Mild to moderate spice. Tasso is TAH-so.

kept.a: Suggest the shrimp and grits to a guest who wants something savory and Southern, to someone who has never had grits, or to a guest looking for value. It suits a warm courtyard day. Pour the Minuty rosé at $17; for a guest who finds the tasso spicy, the Berres Riesling at $14; for a red, the new Barbera at $16; without alcohol, the Personality. Say: “Our Shrimp and Grits has Louisiana shrimp in Creole sauce with tasso, over a crisp fried pimento cheese grit cake.”

New Orleans Shrimp & Grits is a breakfast and lunch entrée at $25, our take on the Southern classic, with a twist.

Instead of a bowl of grits, the grits are made with pimento cheese, set into a cake and fried, so they are crisp outside and creamy inside. Louisiana shrimp go on top in a Creole sauce, a tomato-based sauce with the holy trinity of onion, celery and bell pepper, seasoned with tasso, TAH-so, a smoky, spiced Cajun ham. Fried okra chips go on top for crunch.

The guest gets the golden grit cake under the shrimp and their red sauce, with the okra chips over it all. It tastes creamy and crisp, smoky and tangy, with mild to moderate spice.

It is one of the best values on the menu, and a dish that feels very New Orleans at midday. The Minuty rosé from Provence is the pour: dry and refreshing, bright enough for the tomato and fruity enough for the tasso.

Asked: Is it a bowl of grits?

Answer: No: the grits are made with pimento cheese, set into a cake and fried, crisp outside and creamy inside, with the shrimp on top.

Asked: What is tasso?

Answer: TAH-so: a smoky, spiced Cajun ham that seasons the Creole sauce.

Asked: Is it spicy?

Answer: Mild to moderate, from the tasso and the Creole sauce. The rosé or the Riesling calms it.

Say tasso as the house says it: TAH-so is printed, TASS-oh is also heard, and the house habit is a lineup question. Tell guests the grits come as a fried cake, so nobody expects a creamy bowl. Keep the rosé iced on a warm day and pour it as the entrée fires. Avoid oaky Chardonnay and tannic reds with the shrimp and the smoke. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Pecan Gulf Fish
dishes.serviceNote: Know today’s fish. Fish, shellfish (crab), tree nuts (pecans); likely dairy. Confirm what the kitchen means by bordelaise, the classic French sauce is red wine-based; in New Orleans the word often means garlic butter.

kept.a: Offer the Pecan Gulf Fish to a guest who wants fish at midday, something lighter than eggs, or the local catch. Name today's fish first, then the crab. Pour the Gainey Chardonnay at $17; the Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin is the finer step up; without alcohol, the Oh! What It Seemed to Be. Say: “The Pecan Gulf Fish is today's local catch, topped with lump crab, with a pecan bordelaise, cauliflower purée and collard greens.”

The Pecan Gulf Fish is a breakfast and lunch entrée at $31, our Gulf fish plate, and lighter than the egg dishes.

The fish changes with what is fresh, so the server learns today's catch at lineup. It is topped with Louisiana lump crab, the sweet, meaty pieces from the body of the crab, and sauced with a pecan bordelaise, nutty and savory. In New Orleans, bordelaise often means garlic butter rather than the classic French red wine sauce, and the kitchen confirms which it is. Underneath sit a silky cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens.

The guest gets the fish crowned with crab over the pale purée and dark greens, with the pecan sauce. It tastes nutty, buttery and sweet from the crab, with earthy greens.

It is satisfying without being heavy. The Gainey Estate Chardonnay is the pour, creamy enough for the pecans and crab and fresh enough for the fish; if tonight's bordelaise is red-wine based, the Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir takes its place.

Asked: What is the fish today?

Answer: It changes with what is fresh. I learn it at lineup, so I can tell you exactly.

Asked: What is a pecan bordelaise?

Answer: A nutty, savory pecan sauce. In New Orleans, bordelaise often means garlic butter rather than the French red wine sauce, and the kitchen tells us which it is today.

Asked: What is lump crab?

Answer: The sweet, meaty pieces from the body of the crab.

Know today's fish before service; a guest will ask. Ask the chef whether tonight's bordelaise is garlic butter or red wine based: it decides whether you pour the Gainey or the Bourgogne Pinot Noir. Do not confuse this plate with the Gulf Fish en Papillote, the $38 dinner entrée steamed in a banana leaf. Pour the Gainey around 50°F. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Crab & Corn Omelette
dishes.serviceNote: Shellfish (crab), eggs, dairy (butter), tree nuts (Marcona almonds), soy (miso). A lighter option for guests who don’t want hollandaise.

kept.a: Offer the omelette to a guest who wants eggs without hollandaise, who loves crab, or who wants something lighter at midday. Pour the Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé at $40 by Coravin for a white Burgundy lover; the house Champagne, $30 a glass as the menu prints it, is always right with eggs and crab; without alcohol, the Personality. Say: “Our Crab and Corn Omelette has lump crab and sweet corn, with miso butter, lemon and basil, and a Marcona almond gremolata.”

The Crab & Corn Omelette is a breakfast and lunch entrée at $28, a summer-in-Louisiana omelette and a lighter choice that still feels special.

It is filled with Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn, both naturally sweet, so they suit each other. Our house-made miso butter adds a savory, almost nutty depth, and lemon and basil keep it fresh. On top goes a gremolata, greh-moh-LAH-tah, a bright Italian mix of herbs and citrus zest, made here with Marcona almonds, the rich, tender Spanish almonds, for crunch.

The guest gets a folded omelette with the butter, the herbs and the crunchy topping. It tastes sweet, buttery and savory, with a bright herbal crunch.

It is the egg dish for a guest who does not want hollandaise. The guide pours the Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin with it, white Burgundy rich enough for the crab and butter and bright enough for the lemon; the Gainey Chardonnay is worth offering too, once the sommelier confirms it tastes fresh.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Leflaive at $40 is first pick for a $28 omelette. The guide already uses Gainey first and Leflaive as the step up on the oysters, the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Poussin; the dossier would use the same order on both crab dishes after confirming the Gainey reads fresh rather than oaky. The Leflaive stays first in this pack as the guide prints it.

Asked: What is gremolata?

Answer: Greh-moh-LAH-tah: a bright Italian mix of herbs and citrus zest. Ours is made with Marcona almonds for crunch.

Asked: Is the miso butter made here?

Answer: Yes, it is house-made, and it gives a savory, almost nutty depth.

Asked: Is there hollandaise on it?

Answer: No. It is finished with miso butter, lemon and basil, which makes it the lighter egg dish.

The Leflaive is poured by Coravin: present the bottle and pour through the needle; no cork is pulled. Whether the Gainey Chardonnay tastes fresh rather than oaky is a lineup question for the sommelier, and the answer decides whether you offer it as the lower priced pour. Avoid tannic reds with miso and egg. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak
dishes.serviceNote: Ask temperature, hanger is at its best medium-rare to medium. Eggs (runny yolk, béarnaise), dairy. Mild spice. Different plate from dinner’s Creole Hanger Steak, don’t mix them up.

kept.a: Offer the hanger steak to the guest who wants steak at breakfast or lunch, or a meat lover who finds the egg dishes too light. Ask the temperature as you take the order. Pour the Moulin d'Issan at $16; for a softer red, the Durban at $19; for a celebration, the Inglenook Rubicon 2010 at $70. Without alcohol, the Personality. Say: “Our hanger steak is Creekstone Prime with Creole spice, a smoked potato pavé, a sunny-side-up egg and béarnaise. How would you like it cooked?”

The Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak is a breakfast and lunch entrée at $38, steak and eggs done properly.

Hanger is a butcher's favorite cut, loose-grained and very beefy, and ours is USDA Prime from Creekstone Farms, a Kansas producer of Black Angus beef, seasoned with Creole spice. It comes with a smoked potato pavé, pah-VAY, thin potato slices layered, pressed, cut into a neat block and crisped, a sunny-side-up egg from Vital Farms, whose hens are pasture raised, and classic French béarnaise, bair-NAYZ: butter, egg yolk, shallot and tarragon.

The guest gets the sliced steak beside the crisp potato block, the egg with its runny yolk and the béarnaise. It tastes beefy and spiced, with a smoky, crisp potato and a rich sauce.

It is at its best medium-rare to medium. The Moulin d'Issan Bordeaux Supérieur is the pour: a classic Bordeaux with cassis and cedar and the structure for beef and béarnaise, not too heavy for midday.

Asked: What is a hanger steak?

Answer: A butcher's favorite cut, loose-grained and very beefy. Ours is Prime grade from Creekstone Farms.

Asked: How should I have it cooked?

Answer: Hanger is at its best medium-rare to medium, but it is your call; I write the temperature on the ticket.

Asked: What is a pavé?

Answer: Pah-VAY means paving stone: thin potato slices layered, pressed, cut into a block and crisped, here with a smoky note.

Take the temperature first, and pour the Bordeaux as the steak fires so it has a few minutes to open, at about 60 to 62°F. Do not mix it up with the dinner Creole Hanger Steak, $42, which has broccolini, persillade and chili crisp and no egg. Confirm at lineup that Creekstone Farms and Vital Farms are still the names to say before you name them. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.name: Roasted Chateaubriand
dishes.serviceNote: Serves two, $120. Ask temperature once for the table. A whole roast takes longer, confirm timing with the kitchen and set expectations. Dairy and eggs (Foyot). Ask at lineup whether it’s carved tableside or in the kitchen. Natural side upsells: Maggie’s Mushrooms, Shells & Cheese ($12 each).

kept.a: Offer the Chateaubriand to a couple celebrating, an anniversary, a birthday or two guests who both want beef. It takes longer than a single steak, so offer it early and set the timing honestly. Suggest a side for the table, Maggie's Mushrooms or the Shells & Cheese at $12 each, and the Inglenook Rubicon at $70 the glass; for a red Burgundy from the cellar, bring in the sommelier. Say: “For two of you, the Chateaubriand is our celebration plate: the center of the tenderloin, roasted whole, with sauce Foyot.”

The Roasted Chateaubriand is our dinner centerpiece for two, $120, and a celebration dish.

Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN, is the classic French cut for two: the thickest, most tender center of the beef tenderloin. Ours is Creekstone Farms beef, roasted whole so it stays juicy. It comes with roasted and glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot, fwah-YO, which is béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, made richer with a reduced meat glaze. The sauce is named for the Restaurant Foyot, which stood opposite the Senate in Paris until 1937.

The guest gets the roast with its squash and a sauce rich enough to match it; whether it is carved at the table or in the kitchen is confirmed at lineup. It tastes very tender and buttery, with a savory, rich sauce.

A side of Maggie's Mushrooms or the Shells & Cheese makes it a full feast for two. With it we pour the 2010 Inglenook Rubicon by the glass, a Napa legend whose sixteen years have made it silky.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Aged Cabernet with lean tenderloin and sauce Foyot is textbook. $70 a glass is $140 for two, close to a bottle; the Moulin d'Issan is the classic at $16; name the Beaune as second choice only if it is poured a la carte; the sommelier handoff for a red Burgundy is right.

Asked: What is sauce Foyot?

Answer: Fwah-YO: béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, made richer with a reduced meat glaze.

Asked: How long does it take?

Answer: A whole roast takes longer than a steak. I confirm tonight's timing with the kitchen so you know what to expect before you order.

Asked: Is it carved at the table?

Answer: That is confirmed at lineup each night, and I will check with the kitchen and tell you how it comes.

It serves two at $120: say so plainly before the order. Ask the temperature once for the table. Confirm the cooking time with the kitchen and set expectations, and ask at lineup whether it is carved tableside. At $70 a glass, two glasses of Rubicon cost close to a bottle, so mention the sommelier for a bottle and the Moulin d'Issan at $16 as the classic alternative. The Jadot Beaune is offered only if it is poured à la carte. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

value.sayIt: For the Chateaubriand, we pour the 2010 Inglenook Rubicon by the glass, a Napa legend with real age on it, powerful but silky. Or I can bring our sommelier for a red Burgundy from our cellar.
value.whyThisWine: The Rubicon is a Napa legend with sixteen years of age. It’s powerful, but the age has made it silky, so it flatters the tenderness of the beef and loves the rich Foyot sauce.
value.palate: Tenderloin is lean, so a young, firm Cabernet would dry the palate. Here age has softened the tannin; it binds with the Foyot’s butter and the beef’s protein and feels round. The meat glaze’s savory depth meets the wine’s tertiary earth and tobacco, while its cassis fruit gives the mild beef a lift. Acidity cuts the béarnaise, and the finish stays long, savory and silky.
value.secondWhy: For finesse over power: a Premier Cru red Burgundy, tenderloin is delicate, and Pinot Noir lets it shine.
value.serve: $70 by the glass. Keep the bottle upright and pour gently to leave any sediment behind. Bordeaux glass, 60 to 64°F. For a red Burgundy from the cellar, bring in the sommelier.
value.avoid: Avoid young, high-tannin, heavily oaked reds: lean tenderloin can’t soften that tannin, and the oak buries the Foyot.
value.zeroProofWhy: tart cherry stands in for a red wine’s fruit, and the bubbles cut the Foyot’s butter.

dishes.name: Redfish Véronique
dishes.serviceNote: Fish, dairy (beurre blanc). Redfish is a firm, mild Gulf fish. On the dinner tasting it’s paired with Louis Jadot Beaune 1er Cru, a good talking point for red with fish.

kept.a: Offer the Véronique to a guest who wants fish at dinner, something elegant and light, or a French classic with a local fish. Pour the Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé at $40 by Coravin à la carte. Say: “Our Redfish Véronique is Louisiana redfish with hibiscus-pickled grapes, braised leeks and a preserved lemon butter sauce.”

The Redfish Véronique is a dinner entrée at $36, and the third course of our $80 dinner tasting.

Véronique, vay-ro-NEEK, is the French classic of fish with grapes. We make it with Louisiana redfish, a firm, mild Gulf fish that cooks up flaky. The grapes are pickled with hibiscus, so they are sweet, tart and floral. Braised leeks are soft and gently sweet, fingerling potatoes make it satisfying, and a beurre blanc, burr BLAHN, a silky butter sauce made with white wine, gets its brightness from preserved lemon.

The guest gets the fish over leeks and potatoes, the pickled grapes around it and the butter sauce. It tastes buttery and flaky, with sweet-tart grapes and bright lemon.

It is elegant and balanced, a classic idea with a Louisiana fish. À la carte, the Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin is the pour, since beurre blanc and white Burgundy are a classic. On the tasting it is paired with a light red, the Louis Jadot Beaune 1er Cru, whose red fruit loves the hibiscus grapes.

Answer: Vay-ro-NEEK: the French classic of fish with grapes. Ours are pickled with hibiscus.

dishes.name: Gulf Fish en Papillote
dishes.serviceNote: Know today’s fish. Fish, shellfish (crab), tree nuts (Marcona almonds). Sorghum is gluten-free, but confirm the whole dish. Ask at lineup whether it’s opened at the table, if so, warn guests about the steam.

Pour the Albariño at $16; the Minuty rosé at $17 is the alternative for the tomato and olive; without alcohol, the Oh! What It Seemed to Be. Say: “Our Gulf Fish en Papillote is baked in a banana leaf so it steams in its own juices, with crab, olives, tomato and Marcona almonds.”

The Gulf Fish en Papillote is a dinner entrée at $38, and a lighter plate that is still full of flavor.

En papillote, ahn pah-pee-YOHT, means cooked sealed in a wrapper, classically paper; here the wrapper is a banana leaf, so the fish steams gently in its own juices and stays very moist. The fish changes with what is fresh. Inside the leaf go Louisiana crab for sweetness, tomato, Castelvetrano olives, kah-stel-veh-TRAH-noh, the bright green, mild and buttery Sicilian olives, Marcona almonds, and sorghum, a chewy ancient grain.

The guest gets the parcel itself, and inside it moist fish with the crab, olives and tomato; whether it is opened at the table is confirmed at lineup. It tastes moist and delicate, bright and Mediterranean, with nutty crunch.

The banana leaf is the house's own touch on a classic method. The Pazo das Bruxas Albariño is the pour, citrusy with a salty edge, made for seafood with olives and tomato.

dishes.serviceNote: Poultry; dairy (cream sauce), mustard; likely gluten (fried coating), confirm. Whole small bird; may have bones.

The Poussin à la Moutarde is a dinner entrée at $29, where a French bistro meets a Southern kitchen, and one of the best values on the dinner menu.

Poussin, poo-SAN, à la moutarde means young chicken with mustard. Ours is a Cornish hen, brined in sweet tea, which seasons it and keeps it juicy, then fried until crisp. The classic French partner is mustard, so it comes with a mustard cream sauce, tangy and rich, with turnips and shallots for a gentle sweetness.

The guest gets a whole small bird, fried golden, with the creamy sauce and the vegetables; as a whole bird, it may have bones. It tastes crisp, juicy and savory, with a tangy, creamy sauce.

It is Southern fried chicken dressed for a French table, and comforting. The Gainey Estate Chardonnay is the pour, creamy enough for the mustard sauce and fresh enough for the fried crust, and the Pierre Sparr sparkling rosé is a co-equal, because bubbles and fried chicken are a classic.

dishes.serviceNote: Soy. Ask the kitchen whether it’s fully vegan, blackening is traditionally done with butter, and whether the rice grits use any stock. Rice is naturally gluten-free; confirm the spice blend and mushrooms. Moderate spice.

Say: “Our Blackened Tofu is New Orleans tofu with a spiced crust, over Two Brooks Farm rice grits with preserved shiitake mushrooms.”

The Blackened Tofu is a dinner entrée at $25, and the plate for a guest who wants a meatless entrée, once the kitchen has confirmed how it is made tonight.

The tofu comes from Tien Dat, a Vietnamese family co-op across the river that presses it fresh every week. We blacken it, the Louisiana technique of coating in spices and searing in a very hot pan, so it gets a dark, spiced crust. It sits over rice grits from Two Brooks Farm, a family rice farm at Sumner in the Mississippi Delta: broken grains of rice cooked creamy like grits. Preserved shiitake mushrooms, shee-TAH-keh, bring deep, savory flavor.

The guest gets the dark-crusted tofu over creamy grits with the mushrooms. It tastes spiced and crusty outside, soft inside, earthy and savory, with moderate spice.

It shows the kitchen's local sourcing. The Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir is the pour: light and silky with an earthy note that loves mushrooms, and low tannin that will not clash with the spice.

The Creole Hanger Steak is a dinner entrée at $42, bold, spiced and fun.

Hanger is a butcher's favorite cut, loose-grained and very beefy, and ours is Creekstone Farms beef seasoned with our own housemade Creole spice. Broccolini is glazed with Madeira, the fortified wine, so it is a little sweet and nutty. Persillade, pair-see-YAHD, is chopped parsley and garlic, and we add pepitas, pumpkin seeds, for crunch. The guest gets sliced steak with the glossy broccolini, the green persillade and the chili crisp over it. It tastes beefy and spiced, with crunch, heat and a sweet-savory glaze.

It is the dinner hanger, spicier than the daytime one and with no egg. The Domaine de Durban Beaumes-de-Venise Rouge is the pour: ripe and generous, with soft tannins and a peppery note that love a little spice, served cool so its alcohol does not lift the heat.

The Housemade Pork Sausage Patty is a breakfast and lunch side at $9, and the one breakfast meat we make ourselves.

We make our own pork sausage in house and form it into a patty, the classic Southern breakfast way. A Southern breakfast sausage is traditionally fresh pork shoulder seasoned with salt, black pepper and sage, often with red pepper and a touch of brown sugar; what goes into ours, and how much heat it carries, is a question for the kitchen.

It belongs to the breakfast Owen Brennan made the event: in a city whose restaurants served lunch and dinner, he made breakfast the reason to come, and the sides are how a guest builds that breakfast out. The Buttermilk Biscuit is a breakfast and lunch side at $5.

A buttermilk biscuit is the Southern breakfast bread. The classic method is soft flour and cold butter or lard, buttermilk reacting with baking soda to lift the dough, a few folds for layers and a hot oven. The buttermilk makes it tender and gives it a gentle tang. How ours is made each morning is a question for the kitchen.

The guest gets a warm biscuit, golden outside, soft and layered within. It tastes tender, buttery and a little tangy.

Its real job at Brennan's is the sauce. The Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen both carry hollandaise and marchand de vin, and a biscuit finishes every last bit of both. It also rounds out a lighter plate, such as the omelette, for a hungry guest.

The menu prints the biscuit alone, so butter or jam with it is confirmed with the kitchen. Offer it as the eggs are ordered, so it lands warm with them.

The Cheddar Grits are a breakfast and lunch side at $7, the Southern breakfast staple.

Grits are coarsely ground corn, cooked slowly until creamy, the Southern answer to polenta. Ours have cheddar stirred in, so they are rich and a little sharp.

The guest gets a warm bowl of creamy, pale gold grits. They taste creamy, rich and a little sharp from the cheese, with the gentle sweetness of corn.

They are the side for a guest who has never had grits, because cheese makes them friendly, and for anyone who wants Southern comfort beside the eggs. An egg any style on top turns them into a small meal, and they sit well beside the thick-cut bacon or the housemade sausage patty.

They are not the grit cake on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits: that one is made with pimento cheese, set and fried. And they are not the rice grits under the Blackened Tofu at dinner, which are broken rice from Two Brooks Farm.

kept.a: Offer Brabant potatoes with any egg dish, the bacon or the sausage, and to a guest who wants something crisp and familiar beside the sauces. They are the friendliest side for a visitor: everyone loves crisp potatoes, and the name gives you a story. Say: “Can I add Brabant potatoes? They're the old New Orleans side: crisp cubes of potato, finished with garlic and parsley.” For a shared table, one bowl goes a long way.

Brabant Potatoes are a breakfast and lunch side at $7, and an old New Orleans restaurant classic.

They have been in the Picayune's Creole Cook Book since the early 1900s, and they are usually said to be named for the Brabant region of Belgium and the Netherlands. Potatoes are cut into cubes and cooked until golden and crisp outside and fluffy inside, then traditionally finished with garlic butter and parsley; the kitchen confirms tonight's finish at lineup.

The guest gets a bowl of golden cubes, flecked with green. They taste crisp, fluffy, buttery and garlicky.

They are the side every egg dish wants, and the best partner for the housemade sausage or the thick-cut bacon. An egg any style with a bowl of Brabant potatoes makes a small breakfast of its own. They also appear on the children's breakfast menu, with the popcorn shrimp and the grilled cheese.

The name trips people up: the guide prints bra-BAHNT, and bra-BAHN and the local bruh-BANT are both heard, so learn the house's way at lineup.

Asked: What are Brabant potatoes?

Answer: An old New Orleans side: cubes of potato cooked golden and crisp outside, fluffy inside, traditionally finished with garlic butter and parsley.

Asked: Where does the name come from?

Answer: They are usually said to be named for the Brabant region of Belgium and the Netherlands, though no one has proved it. They have been in New Orleans Creole cookbooks since the early 1900s.

Asked: How do you say it?

Answer: The guide prints bra-BAHNT; bra-BAHN and bruh-BANT are both heard here. I say it the way the house does.

Say: “The succotash is glazed summer vegetables with Nueske's bacon, sweet and smoky, lovely with the Chateaubriand.” For a table of two sharing the Chateaubriand, it is the vegetable to add beside the mushrooms.

The Succotash is a dinner side at $12, and a seasonal one.

Succotash is a Native American dish of corn and beans, some four hundred years old, that the South adopted; traditionally it is corn and lima beans. Ours is a mix of glazed summer vegetables with Nueske's bacon, a Wisconsin bacon known since 1933 for its deep applewood smoke.

The guest gets a bowl of bright, glossy vegetables with pieces of smoky bacon through them. It tastes sweet and bright from the glazed vegetables, savory and smoky from the bacon.

It is a great partner for the Roasted Chateaubriand or the Poussin à la Moutarde, and a way to bring something green and seasonal to a rich dinner.

It changes with the season: the dinner menu is a late summer one, and tonight's vegetables are confirmed at lineup. It is not a meatless side, because of the bacon, so say so when a guest asks for vegetables.

Answer: Glazed summer vegetables with Nueske's bacon. The vegetables change with the season, and I learn tonight's at lineup.

Asked: Is it a traditional succotash?

Answer: Traditionally succotash is corn and lima beans, a Native American dish the South adopted. Ours is a summer vegetable version with bacon.

The Shells & Cheese is a dinner side at $12: our grown-up mac and cheese.

Pasta shells hold the sauce in every curve, and the sauce is a fondue of Mimolette, mee-mo-LET, a bright orange French cheese from Lille, nutty and a little sweet as it ages. It is made with Abita Amber, the Louisiana lager brewed at Abita Springs since 1986, for a malty depth, and finished with Grana Padano, the hard, nutty Italian cheese, for a salty finish.

dishes.name: World Famous Bananas Foster
dishes.serviceNote: Minimum 2 people per order ($14). Seed it with the entrée order. The printed menu says rum; Brennan’s own published recipe also uses banana liqueur, follow the house procedure you’re trained on. TABLESIDE SAFETY: (1) Set the cart where nothing hangs overhead and away from drapes, décor and air vents; clear menus, napkins and paper from it. (2) Guests seated and back from the cart; no one leaning in; watch children, loose sleeves and long hair. (3) Measure the rum into a small vessel first, never pour from the bottle near a flame. (4) Pull the pan off the flame to add rum, then tilt the far edge toward the flame to ignite, away from you and the guests. (5) Never add alcohol to a lit pan. (6) Keep a lid or cover within reach to smother, and know where the extinguisher is. (7) Let the flame burn out before plating; turn the burner off before you leave the cart. Flambéing doesn’t remove all the alcohol, tell guests who avoid it. Dairy (butter, ice cream); ice cream likely contains egg. On the breakfast tasting it comes with Congregation Coffee & Chicory.

kept.q: Does the recipe use banana liqueur as well as rum?
kept.a: Our published recipe uses both banana liqueur and rum, in equal measure; the menu prints rum. Say rum and a splash of banana liqueur once the kitchen confirms the cart build.

Seed Bananas Foster with the entrée order, so the cart is ready: every first visit, every celebration, every guest who asks what Brennan's is famous for. Remind the table it is for two or more. With it, the Dr. Hermann Auslese half-bottle at $80 when the sommelier confirms it is still poured, or a cup of our coffee with chicory at $11. Say: “Save room for Bananas Foster: it was invented here in 1951, and we flambé it right at your table.”

World Famous Bananas Foster is the dessert Brennan's gave the world, $14 at every meal, flambéed at the table, with a minimum of two people per order.

It was invented here in 1951. Owen Brennan asked for a banana dessert, and chef Paul Blangé created it; the house's own telling credits Ella Brennan with Blangé. It is named for Owen's friend Richard Foster, chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission, and New Orleans was then the main port for bananas from Central America. 2026 is its 75th year.

At the cart, butter, brown sugar and cinnamon melt into a caramel; banana liqueur goes in as our published recipe has it, then the bananas to soften; then the rum is lit. As it burns, the caramel deepens. The bananas are spooned over our housemade vanilla ice cream, then the warm sauce.

It tastes warm, caramelized and boozy-sweet over cold, creamy vanilla. It closes the Traditional Breakfast with Congregation Coffee & Chicory.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Rum, butter, brown sugar and flambeed caramel sit in the caramel and nut group, whose textbook partners are oxidative fortifieds, so Banyuls Reserva would lead and the Auslese would be the bright second for contrast. The Auslese stays first in this pack because the Banyuls is a tasting pour and is not confirmed a la carte; nothing changes until that answer exists.

Asked: Was it really invented here?

Answer: Yes, in 1951, by chef Paul Blangé at Owen Brennan's request; the house's own telling credits Ella Brennan with him. It is named for Richard Foster, Owen's friend.

Asked: Does the alcohol burn off?

Answer: Not all of it. Flaming leaves much of the alcohol in the sauce, so I tell anyone avoiding alcohol.

Asked: Can I order one for myself?

Answer: It is made in one pan at the table for at least two people, so the minimum order is two. For a flambé just for you, let me ask the manager what the kitchen can do tonight.

A minimum of two per order; whether the $14 is per person or per order is a lineup question, so never quote it either way until a manager says. A new server never lights a pan before sign off: who performs the flambé, and the house procedure, are lineup questions for the manager. Pour any wine before the flambé starts, so no glass sits near the flame. Follow the tableside safety steps in the service note every time. The origin is disputed between the guide and the house page: use the house's telling once a manager confirms it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

The New Orleans Bread Pudding is a dessert at $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: New Orleans' comfort dessert, done our way.

Bread pudding began as an old European thrift dish for stale bread and became a New Orleans staple; the Picayune's Creole Cook Book of 1901 already prints one.
