dishes.serviceNote: Eggs (meringue, mousse), dairy, gluten (pastry). The lightest dessert, suggest it after a rich meal.

kept.a: Offer the Lemon Tart after a rich meal, after the Hussarde or the Chateaubriand, to a guest who says they are too full for dessert, or to someone who loves citrus. Pour the Auslese half-bottle at $80 once you know it is still offered, or keep it light with the Personality at $16. Say: “If you'd like something bright after all that richness, our Lemon Tart is yuzu mousse, lemon jelly and toasted meringue.”

The Lemon Tart is a dessert at $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and the lightest dessert on the menu.

It has everything a lemon meringue tart has, built in layers. A yuzu mousse, YOO-zoo, is the heart of it: yuzu is a fragrant Japanese citrus that tastes like lemon, lime and mandarin at once. With it come a lemon jelly, a sweet pastry crumb for crunch, and toasted meringue, soft and marshmallowy.

The guest gets the layers of pale mousse and bright jelly over the crumb, with the browned meringue on top. It tastes bright, tart and airy, with sweet crunch.

It is the dessert to suggest after a rich meal, when a guest wants something refreshing rather than heavy. Citrus desserts are hard on wine, but a sweet Mosel Riesling loves them: the Dr. Hermann Auslese has the acidity to match the lemon, which is why it is the match, as a half-bottle, and why Banyuls is not.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Confirmed: only sweet plus piercing acid survives the yuzu and lemon; the Banyuls avoid line is right.

Asked: What is yuzu?

Answer: YOO-zoo: a fragrant Japanese citrus that tastes like lemon, lime and mandarin at once.

Asked: Is it a classic lemon tart?

Answer: It has all the flavors of a lemon meringue tart, built in layers: yuzu mousse, lemon jelly, a sweet pastry crumb and toasted meringue.

Asked: Which dessert is lightest?

Answer: This one: tart, airy and refreshing.

Do not pour Banyuls or another low-acid dessert wine with it: lemon makes them taste flabby, and red fruit clashes with yuzu. The Auslese comes only as the $80 half-bottle, 2 to 3 oz pours, unless a manager says it can be poured by the glass. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

dishes.serviceNote: Gluten (puff pastry), dairy, eggs (anglaise, mousse).

kept.a: Offer the tarte Tatin to a guest who loves fruit desserts, who wants something lighter than a flambé, or who knows the French classic. Say: “Our Pineapple Tarte Tatin is the French upside-down tart made with charred pineapple, with a condensed milk anglaise and vanilla mousse.”

The Pineapple Tarte Tatin is a dessert at $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: tropical, buttery and bright.

Tarte Tatin, tart tah-TAN, is the famous French upside-down tart, usually apples caramelized in butter and sugar on crisp pastry. We make it with pineapple, charred so it is caramelized with a little smoky edge, on puff pastry for flaky layers. The anglaise, a pourable vanilla custard, is made with sweetened condensed milk for a rich, caramel-milk flavor, and a whipped vanilla mousse keeps it light.

The guest gets the caramelized pineapple on its pastry, with the custard sauce and the mousse. It tastes caramelized, tangy and flaky, with creamy vanilla.

It is a French classic with a tropical twist, and a lighter alternative to the flambés. The Dr. Hermann Auslese is the pour: it carries pineapple and honey notes of its own, so the wine mirrors the tart, and it stays bright enough to cut the pastry and the custard.

Asked: What is a tarte Tatin?

Answer: Tart tah-TAN: the French upside-down caramelized tart, usually apples. Ours is charred pineapple on puff pastry.

Asked: What is the anglaise?

Answer: A pourable vanilla custard, made here with sweetened condensed milk for a caramel-milk flavor.

Asked: Is it very sweet?

Answer: It is caramelized, but the pineapple's tang and the light vanilla mousse keep it bright.

Avoid Banyuls and dry wines with it: red fruit clashes with pineapple, and dry wines taste sour against the caramel. Pour the Auslese 2 to 3 oz as the dessert fires. Say Tatin as tah-TAN. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

The Roost Burger is the one full plate on the Bubbles at Brennan's bar snack list, $17, served in the Roost Bar and the courtyard on weekday afternoons from 2 to 6.

The current menu prints the build: two beef short rib patties, bacon, cheese, pickles, onions, tomato jam and a special sauce. Short rib is a well marbled, deeply beefy cut, which is why it makes a rich patty. Which cheese, what goes into the special sauce, the bun and how the patties are cooked are questions for the kitchen at lineup.

The guest gets a double burger. It tastes rich and beefy, salty from the bacon, sharp from the pickles and onions, with the sweetness of the tomato jam.

It is the plate for a guest who wants a proper meal at the bar rather than snacks. With it, the Moulin d'Issan, a classic Bordeaux with tannin for the beef, or the Rumors are Flying, our barrel aged Rittenhouse rye with tart cherry juice, brown sugar syrup and orange bitters.

A guest eating in the Roost can also be offered the Flamingo, the Birdcage or the Spoonbill, which are poured only there.

Describe it from the menu's build only: two short rib patties, bacon, cheese, pickles, onions, tomato jam and special sauce. Brennan's Essential by Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut is our house Champagne, poured by the glass at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: $28 a glass on the Binwise list and $30 on the current menu, so the price is confirmed at lineup.

It is a Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut labeled for us, a blend of all three Champagne grapes, Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay, made by the traditional method. Extra Brut means very little added sugar, under six grams a liter, so it is drier than a standard Brut. Piper-Heidsieck spells its own cuvée Essentiel; the dosage and lees age wait on the sommelier confirming which cuvée is in the bottle.

In the glass it is pale and lively, with fine bubbles. It tastes very dry and crisp: citrus, orchard fruit and a little brioche, with a firm, chalky finish.

That dryness and those fine bubbles cut through rich, salty food, which is why it is the first pick with the turtle soup, the Grand Isle Jewel oysters and the Eggs Hussarde, and the second choice with the Louisiana Oysters, the Creole Caesar and the omelette. It is the house bubbles, morning and night.

Answer: Very little added sugar, under six grams a liter, so it is drier than a standard Brut.

Asked: Is it made for Brennan's?

Answer: It is a Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut labeled for us. I say labeled for us, not made for us, until the sommelier confirms which cuvée is in the bottle.

Asked: What does it go with?

wines.name: Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d’Alsace NV

kept.a: Show the label and say it as pee-AIR SHPAR. Serve it at 43 to 46°F in a flute or tulip, from an ice bucket half ice and half water. Hold the cork and cage together and ease the cork out quietly. Tilt the glass and pour in two stages so the creamy mousse does not overflow, guests first and the host last. Say: “The Pierre Sparr, a sparkling rosé from Alsace: all Pinot Noir, dry and berry-bright.”

Offer the Pierre Sparr to a guest who wants something pink and festive, at brunch celebrations, and with the steak tartare cannoli, the fried hen and the Sardou or the Owen. It is the friendlier-priced bubbles beside the house Champagne. Say: “If you'd like something pink and festive, the Pierre Sparr is a sparkling rosé from Alsace, made like Champagne, dry with bright berry fruit.”

The Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d'Alsace is our sparkling rosé by the glass, $18 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Pierre Sparr, pee-AIR SHPAR, is an Alsace house. Crémant means the wine is made the same way as Champagne, with the second fermentation in the bottle, and in Alsace a rosé crémant must be all Pinot Noir.

In the glass it is pink and lively, with a creamy mousse. It tastes dry, with strawberry and red currant.

It is Champagne's method at a friendlier price, and the red fruit is what makes it useful at the table: it is the first pick with the Steak Tartare Cannoli, where red fruit suits the raw beef and the bubbles cut the fried shell and the crème fraîche. It is also the second choice with the Eggs Sardou, the Eggs Owen and the Poussin à la Moutarde, and a natural for a brunch celebration.

For a guest who wants bubbles but something pink with the Hussarde, it is all Pinot Noir and dry, with red fruit for the marchand de vin.

Asked: What is a crémant?

Answer: A sparkling wine made the same way as Champagne, with the second fermentation in the bottle, from outside Champagne. This one is from Alsace.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is a Brut: dry, with strawberry and red currant fruit.

Asked: What grape is it?

Answer: All Pinot Noir: in Alsace a rosé crémant must be.

Say Pierre Sparr as pee-AIR SHPAR. It is a sparkling rosé, not Champagne: never call it Champagne. The creamy mousse foams quickly, so pour in two stages. It is not a match for the sweet starters: the curds and the coulis make it taste tart. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Bring the bottle to the table and present the label: the guest is paying for the name. Serve it at 46 to 50°F, a touch warmer than the house bubbles so the vintage complexity shows, in a tulip or white-wine glass. Lift the Coravin Sparkling stopper, pour, and reseal it straight away. Say the vintage only once you have read it on the label. Say: “This is Rare, the prestige vintage: toasted almond and candied citrus. Happy celebration.”

Offer Rare to a table celebrating, an anniversary or a guest who loves Champagne, as the step up from the house glass with the oysters, the turtle soup or the Hussarde. Tell them it is a rare chance to taste a wine like this without buying the bottle. Say: “For a special occasion, we pour Rare by the glass: a prestige vintage Champagne with toasted almond and candied citrus.”

Rare Brut 2012 is our prestige vintage Champagne by the glass, $75 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, poured from a bottle kept fresh under a Coravin Sparkling stopper.

Rare began as Piper-Heidsieck's prestige cuvée and is now run as its own house, Rare Champagne; its first vintage was 1976, and only about a dozen vintages have ever been declared. It is Chardonnay-led, with Pinot Noir, from a single vintage and Grand Cru sites, with about ten years on its lees. Because the opened bottle sits under a Coravin Sparkling stopper, which re-pressurizes it, a single glass is possible.

In the glass it is golden, with a long, fine mousse. It tastes of white peach, candied citrus and toasted almond.

It is the celebration step up: from the house Champagne with the turtle soup, the oysters, the Hussarde and the omelette, and wonderful with crab claws or on its own. The Binwise list and the Birthday Bubbles page print 2012, and the current Wines by the Glass page a 2013 Millésime, so the open vintage is read at lineup.

Answer: A prestige vintage Champagne that began at Piper-Heidsieck and is now its own house; only about a dozen vintages have ever been declared.

Brut means dry, and dry bubbles cut salt and fat, so it is lovely with the Louisiana Oysters, the popcorn shrimp or the fries at Bubbles. It is printed on our Birthday Bubbles page too, a fine glass to toast the 80th.

kept.a: Show the label and say C.H. Berres as BEH-ress. Serve it at 45 to 48°F in a white-wine glass, with no decanting, and keep the bottle well chilled between pours. Pour a standard glass for the guests first and the host last. If the guest asked about sweetness, tell them what you tasted at lineup. Say: “The Berres Riesling, from old vines in the Mosel: light, racy and a touch sweet.”

Offer the Berres with anything spicy: the gumbo, the shrimp and grits, the dinner hanger or the tofu, and with the duck confit waffle. It is a $14 glass, an easy yes. Say: “With anything spicy I love the Berres Riesling from the Mosel: light, racy and a touch sweet, so it cools the heat.” For a guest who says they do not like sweet wine, explain the touch of sweetness is what tames the spice.

The C.H. Berres Old Vines Riesling 2022 is our Riesling by the glass, $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and one of the two least expensive glasses on the list.

C.H. Berres, BEH-ress, is an old Mosel family estate at Ürzig in the Middle Mosel, with roots to 1510. This is Riesling from old vines on the Mosel slate, fermented to leave a touch of sweetness: about twenty grams of sugar a liter, at only 11.5% alcohol.

In the glass it is pale and bright. It tastes light-bodied, with green apple, peach, a slaty mineral note and racy acidity under that touch of sweetness.

That little sweetness is what cools spice, and the low alcohol keeps heat from flaring, so it is the first pick with the Seafood Gumbo and the Duck Confit Waffle, where its fruit meets the maple. It loves the chili crisp on the hanger and the ’nduja on the lobster, and it is the second choice with the baked apple, the lobster, the shrimp and grits and the tofu. Six pairings hinge on how sweet the open bottle tastes, so it is tasted at lineup.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Off-dry: a touch of sweetness, about twenty grams of sugar a liter, balanced by racy acidity. We taste it at lineup, so I can tell you honestly how today's bottle reads.

Asked: Why Riesling with spicy food?

Answer: The touch of sweetness and the low alcohol, 11.5%, cool the heat rather than amplifying it.

Asked: Where is it from?

Answer: An old family estate at Ürzig in Germany's Mosel, from old vines on slate.

Taste the open bottle at lineup and record the label alcohol: six pairings hinge on whether it reads dry or off-dry, and the guide hedges on it. Keep it well chilled with spicy dishes; heat reads hotter with warm wine. Say C.H. Berres as BEH-ress. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say PAH-tho dahs BROO-shas. Serve it at 45 to 48°F in a white-wine glass, with no decanting, and return the bottle to the ice between pours. Pour the guests first and the host last. With the Caesar, mention the smoked oyster dressing as you pour. Say: “The Albariño from Spain's Atlantic coast: lemony and fresh, with a salty edge.”

Offer the Albariño with seafood: the Caesar, the papillote, the oysters for a still wine, and fried seafood at the bar. It suits a guest who likes crisp, dry whites and does not want oak. Say: “The Albariño comes from Spain's Atlantic coast: citrusy, unoaked, with a salty edge made for seafood.”

The Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025 is our Albariño by the glass, $16 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Pazo das Bruxas, PAH-tho dahs BROO-shas, means manor of the witches: it is the Familia Torres estate in Rías Baixas, on the Atlantic coast of Galicia in Spain. Albariño is the crisp, saline white grape of that coast, and this one is unoaked and bottled young for freshness.

In the glass it is pale and bright. It tastes of lemon and white peach, with an almost sea-spray, saline snap, dry and fresh.

That salty freshness makes it a natural with seafood: it is the first pick with the Creole Caesar, whose dressing is made with smoked oysters, and with the Gulf Fish en Papillote, with its olives and tomato; it is the still white offered with the Grand Isle Jewel oysters. It also suits the Marcona almonds on the papillote and the popcorn shrimp at Bubbles.

Its freshness fades as it warms, so it is kept iced between pours.

Asked: What does Pazo das Bruxas mean?

Answer: Manor of the witches. It is the Familia Torres estate in Rías Baixas.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Answer: No: unoaked and bottled young, so it is fresh, with lemon, white peach and a salty snap.

Asked: What goes with it?

Answer: Seafood: the Creole Caesar with its smoked oyster dressing, the Gulf fish en papillote, and oysters if you want a still wine.

Keep it iced between pours: its saline freshness fades as it warms. Confirm at lineup that the vintage is still the 2025, since young whites roll over. Say Pazo das Bruxas as PAH-tho dahs BROO-shas. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Famille Durand Val de Loire Sauvignon Blanc 2024
wines.serviceNote: The current Wines by the Glass page prints Famille Durand, Val de Loire, 2024; the Binwise list read the same day prints Domaine Durand, Loire Valley, 2025, both at $14. Read the label at lineup before naming the producer or the vintage.

kept.a: Show the label and say the producer and vintage as the label reads, Durand as dur-AHN, and name the Loire. Serve it at 45 to 48°F in a white-wine glass, with no decanting, and keep the bottle in the ice bucket. Pour the guests first and the host last. Say: “Our Loire Sauvignon Blanc from the Durand family: crisp, herbal and bone-dry.”

Offer the Durand with the Eggs Sardou above all, and with the tomato tostada, the crab claws and anything herbal. It suits a guest who likes crisp, dry whites, and at $14 it is an easy glass. Say: “Artichokes are tricky with wine, but a Loire Sauvignon Blanc loves them: the Durand is crisp and herbal.”

The Sauvignon Blanc by the glass is our Loire white, $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, one of the two least expensive glasses on the list. The current menu prints it as Famille Durand, Val de Loire, 2024; the Binwise list still prints Domaine Durand, 2025, so the label is read at lineup.

The Durand family, dur-AHN, makes it in France's Loire Valley from Sauvignon Blanc. Val de Loire names the region and no village, so it is called a Loire Sauvignon Blanc, never a Sancerre. The guide described the 2025 as fermented in steel with no oak; the sommelier confirms the 2024.

In the glass it is pale and bright. It tastes bone-dry and zippy, with grapefruit, cut grass and a flinty note.

Artichokes make most wines taste oddly sweet or metallic, but this one's sharp, herbal acidity stands up to them, which is why it is the first pick with the Eggs Sardou. It also loves tomatoes and fresh herbs, so it is the second choice with the Creole Tomato Tostada and the leaner choice with the Louisiana Crab Claws.

Asked: Is it a Sancerre?

Answer: It is a Loire Sauvignon Blanc. The menu prints Val de Loire, the region, and no village, so I never call it Sancerre.

Asked: Why with artichokes?

Answer: Artichokes make most wines taste oddly sweet; a bone-dry, herbal Sauvignon Blanc survives them and joins the artichoke instead.

Asked: Which vintage is it?

Answer: The menu prints 2024 and our wine list 2025, so I read the label before I name it.

The producer and vintage are disputed: the current menu prints Famille Durand, Val de Loire, 2024, and Binwise Domaine Durand, Loire Valley, 2025. Read the label at lineup, and never call it Sancerre. Whether the 2024 is steel fermented with no oak is a lineup question for the sommelier. Keep it in the ice bucket so its acidity stays sharp. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say GAY-nee. Serve it at 50 to 54°F in a larger white or Chardonnay glass, with no decanting; if it is too cold, let it rest out of the ice a few minutes so the creamy texture shows. Pour the guests first and the host last. Say: “The Gainey Chardonnay from Santa Barbara County: creamy, with lemon curd and baked apple, and fresh.”

Offer the Gainey with butter sauces and cream: the BBQ oysters, the pecan fish and the poussin. It suits a guest who asks for Chardonnay or something rounder. The Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé at $40 is the step up for a Burgundy lover. Say: “For something rounder, the Gainey Chardonnay from Santa Barbara County has a creamy texture but stays fresh.”

Gainey farms in both the Santa Ynez Valley and the Sta. Rita Hills and its Chardonnays have carried either appellation; confirm the appellation on the bottle in service. The 'Santa Barbara County' phrase in the say it line is safe either way.

The Gainey Estate Vineyards Chardonnay 2023 is our California Chardonnay by the glass, $17 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Gainey, GAY-nee, is a Santa Barbara County estate that farms in both the Santa Ynez Valley and the Sta. Rita Hills, and its Chardonnays have carried either appellation, so the one on the bottle is confirmed in service. It is cool-climate Chardonnay: the ocean cools the vineyards, which keeps the acidity bright.

In the glass it is golden. It tastes of lemon curd and baked apple, with a creamy texture and bright acidity.

That pairing of creaminess and freshness makes it the first pick for butter and cream: the Louisiana Oysters in their BBQ butter sauce, the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Poussin à la Moutarde with its mustard cream. It is also worth offering with the two crab dishes, keeping the Leflaive as the step up, once the sommelier confirms it tastes fresh rather than oaky.

It is served a little warmer than the crisp whites, so the creamy texture shows.

Asked: Is it oaky?

Answer: It is creamy, from a cool climate that keeps it fresh. Whether today's bottle reads fresh rather than oaky is something the sommelier confirms, and I will check with the sommelier if you dislike oak.

Asked: Where in California?

Answer: Santa Barbara County, where the ocean cools the vineyards; the exact appellation is on the bottle.

Asked: What goes with it?

Answer: Butter and cream: the BBQ oysters, the pecan Gulf fish and the poussin with mustard cream.

Confirm the appellation on the bottle, Sta. Rita Hills or Santa Ynez Valley; Santa Barbara County holds either way. Ask the sommelier whether it reads fresh or oaky: the answer decides whether you offer it on the crab dishes. If it comes out too cold, rest it a few minutes out of the ice. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Present the label first: the estate name matters to Burgundy lovers. Say luh-FLEV, mah-KAWN vair-ZAY. Serve it at 50 to 54°F in a white Burgundy bowl. Pour through the Coravin needle, cork left in, and return the bottle to the cooler. Guests first and the host last. Say: “Domaine Leflaive's Mâcon-Verzé, poured by Coravin: citrus, white flowers and a chalky finish.”

Offer the Leflaive to a white Burgundy lover, with the crab dishes and the redfish, and as the step up from the Gainey. At $40 a glass, name the price and the estate. Say: “If you love white Burgundy, we pour Leflaive's Mâcon by the glass, a legendary estate: rich enough for butter, fresh enough for seafood.”

The Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé 2022 is our white Burgundy by the glass, $40 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, poured by Coravin.

Domaine Leflaive, luh-FLEV, is one of Burgundy's great white-wine estates, best known for Puligny-Montrachet. This is its Chardonnay from Verzé, mah-KAWN vair-ZAY, in the Mâconnais, southern Burgundy. The Coravin is a needle through the cork: the wine is poured without the cork being pulled, which is why a single glass of a wine like this is possible.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of citrus and white flowers, with a fine, chalky texture and a gentle richness.

That balance of richness and freshness is why it is the first pick with the Crab & Corn Omelette, the Louisiana Crab Claws and the Redfish Véronique in its beurre blanc, and the still white offered with the turtle soup. It is the step up from the Gainey with the oysters, the pecan fish and the poussin, and on the lobster course.

The estate's name matters to Burgundy lovers, so the label is always presented.

Asked: Who is Leflaive?

Answer: Luh-FLEV: one of Burgundy's great white-wine estates, best known for Puligny-Montrachet. This is their Mâcon-Verzé.

Asked: How do you pour it by the glass?

Answer: By Coravin: a needle through the cork, so the bottle is never opened and stays fresh.

Asked: Why with the redfish?

Answer: Beurre blanc and white Burgundy are a classic: the wine has the richness for the butter sauce and the brightness for the preserved lemon.

It is poured by Coravin, needle through the cork: never pull the cork, and return the bottle to the cooler after each pour. Which device and log procedure the bar uses is a lineup question. At $40 a glass it is the first pick with a $28 omelette, so offer the Gainey as the lower priced creamy choice once it is confirmed fresh. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

wines.name: Fichet ‘Château London’ Mâcon-Igé 2024

kept.a: Show the label and say fee-SHAY, mah-KAWN ee-ZHAY, once you have confirmed it is tonight's pour. Serve it at 50 to 53°F in a white-wine glass, from a bottle opened at the start of service and kept in a cooler so it does not over-chill. Pour exactly 4 oz just before the lobster lands, guests first and the host last. Say: “With the lobster, a Mâcon-Igé from Domaine Fichet: round enough for the butter, fresh against the spice.”

You sell the Fichet by selling the dinner tasting's $120 pairing; it is the white that meets the lobster. Name it as you pour, and tell the parcel story: guests enjoy that Château London has no castle. If a guest wants a glass on its own, check with the sommelier. Say: “With the lobster we pour a Mâcon from Burgundy: Chardonnay with body for the lobster and a fresh finish.”

The Fichet Château London Mâcon-Igé 2024 is the dinner tasting's white, a 4 oz pour with the Louisiana BBQ Lobster on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Domaine Fichet, fee-SHAY, is a family estate at Igé, mah-KAWN ee-ZHAY, in the Mâconnais, farmed by the Fichet brothers; it is not the Meursault Fichet. Château London is a named vineyard parcel on old limestone, with some vines over a hundred years old: no castle, and nothing to do with England. The wine is made mostly in steel with a touch of old oak.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of apple and citrus, with a gentle roundness and a fresh finish.

That roundness gives it the body for lobster and butter, and the fresh finish lifts the palate after the spicy ’nduja, which is why the guide and the current menu both pour it on that course.

Asked: Is there a castle?

Answer: No. Château London is a named vineyard parcel at Igé, on old limestone; no castle, and nothing to do with England.

Asked: Is it from Meursault?

Answer: No, this Fichet is a family estate at Igé in the Mâconnais, not the Meursault Fichet.

Asked: Can I have a glass on its own?

Answer: It is poured on the tasting pairing and not on the glass list, so I will check with the sommelier.

The guide and the current menu both print this Fichet with the lobster; read the supplement card at lineup all the same. It is an included 4 oz pour on the pairing: never double-pour. Open it at the start of service and keep it in a cooler, not an ice bath. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say mee-nu-TEE. Serve it at 45 to 48°F in a white-wine glass, from an ice bucket half ice and half water, with no decanting. Pour where the guest can see the pale Provence color, guests first and the host last, and return the bottle to the ice. Say: “The Minuty, a classic Provence rosé: pale, dry and refreshing.”

Offer the Minuty on a warm day, in the courtyard, with the tomato tostada, the shrimp and grits and the papillote, and to any guest who asks for rosé. Say: “The Minuty is a classic Provence rosé: pale, dry and refreshing, lovely with tomatoes and shrimp.” Pour it where the guest can see the pale color.

The Minuty Prestige Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024 is our still rosé by the glass, $17 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Minuty, mee-nu-TEE, is one of the classic names of Provence rosé. The Prestige is a Grenache-led wine, pressed pale and bottled young, so it keeps its freshness.

In the glass it is the pale color Provence is known for, and the color is part of the appeal. It tastes dry and refreshing: white peach, wild strawberry and citrus zest, with a light mineral finish.

Its freshness and red fruit are made for tomatoes and shrimp, which is why it is the first pick with the Creole Tomato Tostada, whose raw tomatoes need a wine as bright as they are, and with the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, where the acidity meets the tomato-based Creole sauce and the fruit cushions the tasso. It is the second choice with the Gulf Fish en Papillote for the tomato and olive, and a natural glass in the courtyard on a warm afternoon.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: No, it is dry: white peach, wild strawberry and citrus zest with a light mineral finish.

Asked: Where is it from?

Answer: Provence, in the south of France. Minuty is one of the classic names of Provence rosé.

Asked: What goes with it?

Answer: Tomatoes and shrimp above all: the Creole tomato tostada and the shrimp and grits.

Confirm at lineup that the vintage is still the 2024: young rosé rolls over. Keep it iced, half ice and half water, and pour it well chilled. Say Minuty as mee-nu-TEE. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Offer the Damien Martin to a guest who wants red but a light one: with the tofu, the duck, the egg dishes' marchand de vin and the gumbo. It is the red for breakfast. Say: “If you'd like a red that won't overpower the plate, our Bourgogne Pinot Noir is light and silky with bright cherry fruit.”

The Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir 2023 is our light red Burgundy by the glass, $18 on the current menu at breakfast and lunch and at dinner; the Binwise list still prints $17.

It comes from a father and son family domaine, Domaine Robert et Damien Martin at Davayé in the Mâconnais, southern Burgundy, founded in 1982 by Robert and run by his son Damien, dah-mee-EN mar-TAN.

In the glass it is a translucent ruby. It tastes light and silky: red cherry, raspberry and a touch of earth, with light tannin and fresh acidity.

A light red like this goes where a big red would bully the food. It is the first pick with the Blackened Tofu, whose earthy mushrooms it loves, and the second choice on six plates: the Rohan duck and the duck confit waffle, the steak tartare cannoli, the gumbo, the Eggs Hussarde, where it meets the red wine in the marchand de vin, and the Pecan Gulf Fish if the bordelaise is red-wine based.

It is served slightly cool, around 55 to 58°F, so it stays fresh.

Answer: A light one, yes: the marchand de vin on the Hussarde is a red wine sauce, and this Pinot Noir is light enough for the yolk.

Asked: Where is it from?

Answer: A father and son family domaine at Davayé in the Mâconnais, in southern Burgundy.

Answer: No: light and silky, with red cherry, raspberry and a touch of earth, and light tannin.

kept.a: Show the label and say loo-EE zhah-DOH, BOHN, Premier Cru, once you have confirmed it is tonight's pour. Serve it at 57 to 60°F in a Burgundy bowl, from a bottle opened 20 to 30 minutes ahead. Pour exactly 4 oz just before the redfish lands, guests first and the host last. Say: “With the redfish, a Premier Cru Beaune from Louis Jadot: light and bright, lovely with the grapes.”

You sell the Beaune by selling the dinner tasting's pairing, and by explaining it as it is poured: red with fish surprises guests, and the explanation is the pleasure. For the Chateaubriand table, offer it only if the sommelier confirms it à la carte; otherwise the Moulin d'Issan at $16. Say: “With the redfish we pour a Premier Cru Beaune, a light, bright red Burgundy that loves the pickled grapes.”

The Louis Jadot Beaune 1er Cru 2023 is the dinner tasting's red, a 4 oz pour with the Redfish Véronique on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Louis Jadot, loo-EE zhah-DOH, is the Burgundy house behind it, and Beaune, BOHN, is the wine capital of Burgundy. Premier Cru is Burgundy's second-highest vineyard tier, and the highest in Beaune, which has no Grand Cru. This is Pinot Noir from Premier Cru vineyards there.

In the glass it is bright ruby. It tastes of bright red fruit, with a silky texture and a savory edge.

It is a talking point for red with fish: light enough for the redfish, low in tannin, and its red fruit loves the hibiscus-pickled grapes. It is also the second choice the guide offers with the Chateaubriand, finesse over power, but only if it can be poured à la carte. It is opened 20 to 30 minutes ahead so the young wine shows its perfume.

Asked: Red wine with fish?

Answer: A light red, yes: Pinot Noir with low tannin is gentle with fish, and its red fruit loves the hibiscus-pickled grapes.

Asked: What does Premier Cru mean?

Answer: Burgundy's second-highest vineyard tier, and the highest in Beaune, which has no Grand Cru.

Say: “The Durban, a Southern Rhône red: ripe and generous, with soft tannins for the spice.”

Offer the Durban with the Eggs Owen, the dinner hanger steak and anything spicy or braised, and to a guest who wants a red that is ripe and soft rather than tannic. Say: “The Durban is a Southern Rhône red, ripe and generous with soft tannins, so it handles spice and richness beautifully.”

The Domaine de Durban Beaumes-de-Venise Rouge 2024 is our Southern Rhône red by the glass, $19 on the current menu at breakfast and lunch and at dinner; the Binwise list still prints $18.

Domaine de Durban, dur-BAHN, is famous for its sweet Muscat, but this is the estate's dry red: a Grenache and Syrah blend from the Beaumes-de-Venise cru, BOHM duh vuh-NEEZ, in the Southern Rhône.

In the glass it is deep ruby. It tastes ripe and generous: dark cherry, plum, dried herbs and pepper, with round, soft tannins.

That ripeness and pepper stand up to spice and braise. It is the first pick with the Eggs Owen, whose short rib is braised in red wine under a red wine sauce, and with the Creole Hanger Steak and its chili crisp, where soft tannins keep the heat from turning bitter. It is the second choice with the daytime Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak. The sommelier may also suggest it with the duck on the dinner tasting.

Grenache is generous in alcohol, so a few minutes in the ice bucket keeps it in check with spicy plates.

Asked: Isn't Beaumes-de-Venise a sweet wine?

Answer: The village is famous for sweet Muscat, but this is Durban's dry red, Grenache with Syrah.

Asked: Will it be too strong for the spice?

Answer: Its tannins are soft and its fruit ripe, so it soothes the chili; we serve it a little cool so the alcohol does not lift the heat.

Asked: What does it taste like?

Answer: Dark cherry, plum, dried herbs and pepper, with round tannins.

The glass price is disputed: the current menu prints $19 and Binwise $18, so confirm at lineup and quote the list in hand. Serve it at 58 to 62°F, and with the chili crisp a few minutes in the ice bucket: warm Grenache makes heat burn. Say Beaumes-de-Venise as BOHM duh vuh-NEEZ, and never call it sweet. The printed 2024 blend is a lineup question for the sommelier. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

kept.a: Show the label and say shah-toh-MAR, Cuvée Vincent, and read the vintage off the label: the menu prints 2023. Serve it at 58 to 60°F in a standard red glass, with no decanting. Domaine de Châteaumar's Cuvée Vincent Côtes du Rhône is the breakfast tasting's red, a 4 oz pour with the Petite Filet Mignon on the Traditional Breakfast; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Châteaumar, shah-toh-MAR, grows it as all Syrah from fifty year old vines on two parcels beside Châteauneuf-du-Pape, nine kilometers from Orange, farmed organically without certification. That is unusual in the south, where Grenache usually leads.

In the glass it is deep purple-red. It tastes juicy and soft: black raspberry, black pepper and gentle tannins.

It is just right for red meat at breakfast: its soft tannins meet the lean filet gently, its pepper picks up the garlic spinach, and its freshness cleans up the crisp rösti. It is served slightly cool, 58 to 60°F, to stay fresh in the morning.

The menu prints the 2023; read the label before naming it, and remember it is the Côtes du Rhône, not the estate's Châteauneuf of the same name.

La Miraja Le Masche Barbera d'Asti 2023 is the newest red on our by-the-glass list, $16 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and our one Italian glass.

Barbera, bar-BEAR-ah, is the grape, and Asti the hill country of Piemonte in northwest Italy where it grows; La Miraja is the producer and Le Masche the name of the wine. How long it spends in barrel, and what Le Masche means, are questions for the sommelier.

Inglenook Rubicon 2010 is our grand red by the glass, $70 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Rubicon is Inglenook's flagship, a Cabernet Sauvignon based wine from Rutherford in the Napa Valley, and our glass is the 2010, sixteen years old: a Napa legend with real age on it.

In the glass it is deep garnet. Age has softened the tannins, so it tastes powerful but silky: blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and earth.

That depth is made for the Roasted Chateaubriand and its sauce Foyot, whose lean tenderloin a young, firm Cabernet would dry out, and it suits both hanger steaks. It is the step up with the Petite Filet Mignon on the breakfast tasting and with the daytime hanger.

An older wine can throw sediment, so the bottle is kept upright and poured slowly, leaving the last inch behind, and the label is always presented. At $70 a glass, two glasses come close to a bottle, which is when the sommelier is the better call. How the open bottle is preserved between pours is confirmed at lineup.

The Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet Sauvignon 2021 is the dinner tasting's red, a 4 oz pour with the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Paul Hobbs is the Napa winemaker behind it, and Coombsville, KOOMZ-vil, is one of Napa's cooler corners, near the town of Napa, so its Cabernet keeps its freshness.

In the glass it is deep, dark red. It tastes of dark fruit and cocoa on a firm structure.

The guide's reasoning is that duck breast is red and fatty enough to carry Cabernet: the tannin binds with the fat and the wine tastes rounder, the dark fruit meets the glazed peaches, and the candied hazelnuts echo the cocoa. A young Napa Cabernet against cane syrup peaches is a real tension, which is why the Damien Martin Pinot Noir stands as the lighter alternative.

It is young, so it is opened or decanted 30 to 60 minutes ahead. The duck plate itself is disputed, so the garnish it meets is confirmed with the kitchen.

Answer: One of Napa's cooler corners, near the town of Napa, so the Cabernet keeps its freshness.

Asked: Cabernet with duck?

The Dr. Hermann Erdener Prälat Riesling Auslese 2014 is our sweet wine, sold as a 375 ml half-bottle at $80, at breakfast and lunch and at dinner; it is the only sweet wine sold à la carte.

Dr. Hermann, HAIR-mahn, is the Mosel estate behind it. Auslese, OWS-lay-zuh, means selected harvest, a tier above late-harvest Spätlese, and the fruit comes from the steep Erdener Prälat vineyard, one of the Mosel's famous slopes. Twelve years of age add depth.

In the glass it is golden. It tastes of apricot, honey and pineapple, with electric acidity that keeps the sweetness lively.

Because it is sweeter than our desserts, it never tastes sour beside them, so it is the first pick on seven plates: Bananas Foster, the bread pudding, the Lemon Tart, the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, and the sweet breakfast starters, the trifle, the Framboise French Toast and the baked apple. The half-bottle pours about four dessert glasses of 2 to 3 oz, so it is a wine to share and carry from a sweet starter to dessert.

Answer: It is sold as the $80 half-bottle, about four dessert glasses. Whether a single pour can be rung is a manager's call, so I will check before promising it.

Asked: What does Auslese mean?

Answer: OWS-lay-zuh: selected harvest, a tier above late-harvest Spätlese, so it is sweet and honeyed.

Asked: Will it be too sweet with dessert?

Answer: Its electric acidity keeps it bright, and because it is sweeter than the dessert, the dessert tastes fruitier, not sour.

kept.a: Show the label and say lah TOOR vee-AY, bahn-YOOLS. Serve it slightly cool, about 55°F, in a small dessert glass: 4 oz on the tasting, 2 to 3 oz otherwise, with no decanting. Pour it before the dessert lands, guests first and the host last. Say: “To close, Banyuls from La Tour Vieille: fig, caramel and coffee, the classic with chocolate.”

Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva is the dinner tasting's dessert wine, a 4 oz pour with The Snickers on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Banyuls, bahn-YOOLS, is a sweet fortified red, a vin doux naturel, from the schist terraces around Banyuls-sur-Mer in Roussillon, French Catalonia. It must be at least half Grenache noir, and the fermentation is stopped with neutral grape spirit so the grape's own sugar stays in the wine. La Tour Vieille, lah TOOR vee-AY, ages its Reserva the oxidative way.

In the glass it is a deep, browning red. It tastes of dried fig, walnut, caramel, coffee and orange peel.

It is the classic wine for chocolate: its sweetness keeps chocolate from turning it bitter, and its cocoa and coffee notes echo the dessert. It is the first pick with The Snickers, the Cherries Jubilee and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, and the sommelier may lead with it on Bananas Foster and the bread pudding, once a manager confirms it is poured outside the tasting.

Asked: What is Banyuls?

Answer: Bahn-YOOLS: a sweet fortified red from Roussillon, in French Catalonia, mostly Grenache. Grape spirit stops the fermentation so the wine stays sweet.

Asked: Is it like port?

Answer: It is made in a similar way, a fortified sweet red, but from Grenache in the south of France.

Asked: Can I order a glass?

Answer: It is poured on the dinner tasting; whether it is poured à la carte is a question for the sommelier, so I will check.

Whether it is poured à la carte, at breakfast or at dinner, and at what price, is a sommelier question: until it is answered, the coffee cake, the Jubilee and the Snickers are coffee only à la carte. kept.a: Offer the milk punch at the greeting, before the menus are even open: it is the first sale of the morning and the classic way to start. No house recipe page for the Brandy Milk Punch is published; quote the four menu ingredients only: brandy, heavy cream, vanilla bean, nutmeg.

The Brandy Milk Punch is a Brennan's signature drink, $12 at breakfast and lunch, and the eye opener that begins the Traditional Breakfast.

In New Orleans a proper breakfast starts with an eye opener, and the milk punch is the classic. The menu prints four things: brandy, heavy cream, vanilla bean and nutmeg. The bar shakes the brandy with the cream and real vanilla bean, serves it cold, and finishes it with nutmeg on top. No house recipe is published, so the server quotes those four and no measures.

The guest gets a cold, pale, creamy drink with the nutmeg dusted over it. It tastes creamy, smooth and a little sweet, gently boozy: think of a lighter, boozier eggnog without the egg.

It is the first sale of the morning, offered at the greeting, and the opening course of the $80 tasting, before the baked apple. For a guest who skips it, the Café Glacé de la Maison takes its place without alcohol.

Asked: What is an eye opener?

Answer: The New Orleans tradition of a drink to start breakfast. The Brandy Milk Punch is the classic one.

Asked: What is in it?

Answer: Brandy, heavy cream, vanilla bean and nutmeg, shaken and served cold. The house does not publish measures, so that is all I quote.

Asked: Is it like eggnog?

Answer: A lighter, boozier eggnog without the egg: creamy, smooth and a little sweet.

On the Traditional Breakfast the milk punch is included as course one: never charge it, and pour it at the greeting so the tasting starts on time. Quote only the four menu ingredients; no house recipe is published. Watch the table's intake across the tasting, and offer the Café Glacé de la Maison to a guest who skips alcohol. Do not confuse it with the Prisoner of Love on the fall list, a gin drink made with clarified heavy cream. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

The Bloody Bull is a Brennan's signature drink, $13 at breakfast and lunch, and the drink poured with the soup course on the Traditional Breakfast.

It is a Bloody Mary with beef bouillon stirred in: vodka, our housemade Bloody Mary mix and bouillon, a clear, savory beef broth. The guide calls it a Brennan's breakfast classic, and that is how a server says it. Where it was first made is not something we tell as fact: a guest who asks gets a manager's answer, never a claim that it was invented here.

The guest gets a deep red, savory drink. It tastes savory, rich and meaty, almost like a spicy, chilled consommé, with the spice of the house mix.

It is wonderful with the turtle soup, which is why the tasting pairs them. For a guest who would rather not have beef, the Brennan's Bloody Mary at $11, with pickled okra and spicy beans, is the classic alternative.

Asked: What makes it a Bull?

Answer: Beef bouillon, a clear, savory beef broth, stirred into a Bloody Mary with our housemade mix and vodka.

Asked: Was it invented here?

Answer: It is a Brennan's breakfast classic; I will check with a manager before telling its history.

Asked: Is it spicy?

Answer: The spice comes from our housemade mix. If you are sensitive to heat, I will ask the bar how it is running today.

It carries beef: say so plainly, and offer the Brennan's Bloody Mary to a guest who skips beef, asking the bar about the mix. Never say it was invented here; call it a Brennan's breakfast classic and leave its history to a manager. On the Traditional Breakfast it is the included soup course drink: do not charge it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Classic Sazerac
cocktails.serviceNote: Spirit-forward and strong, served without ice (confirm the glass and the bar’s build). Upsells: Thompson’s Dream ($20, Willett 4-year rye, Bitter Truth Creole Bitters, St. George absinthe rinse) and Origin Story ($40, Dudognon Cognac, barrel-aged Peychaud’s, Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe). Herbsaint is ERB-saint.

kept.a: Offer the Sazerac to whiskey drinkers, to anyone who asks for a New Orleans cocktail, and before dinner. Then climb the ladder: Thompson's Dream at $20 for a richer rye, Origin Story at $40 for the Cognac original. Say: “The Sazerac is New Orleans' official cocktail: Sazerac rye and Peychaud's bitters, in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint.” For a curious guest, describe all three rungs and let them choose.

The Classic Sazerac is a Brennan's signature drink, $13 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and New Orleans' own cocktail.

The Louisiana Legislature named it the official cocktail of New Orleans in 2008: the city's, not the state's. Ours is Sazerac rye whiskey stirred with Peychaud's, PAY-shoze, the bright red New Orleans bitters with anise and cherry notes, and served without ice in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint, ERB-sant, the anise liqueur created in New Orleans in 1934. The rinse gives its aroma without much of its flavor. Sugar and lemon peel are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a short, amber, iceless drink with an anise perfume. It tastes spirit-forward, spicy and aromatic, and strong.

It is the first rung of the house's Sazerac ladder: $13, then Thompson's Dream at $20 with Willett rye, then Origin Story at $40 with Cognac and absinthe, the way the first Sazeracs were made. It suits the guest before dinner or with the steak.

Asked: Is it really the official cocktail?

Answer: Yes, of the city of New Orleans, named by the Louisiana Legislature in 2008; the city's, not the state's.

Asked: What is Herbsaint?

Answer: ERB-sant: an anise liqueur created in New Orleans in 1934. It is only a rinse in the glass, for aroma.

Asked: Can I have it on the rocks?

Answer: It is served without ice. I will check with the bar before promising it on the rocks.

kept.q: What is the classic Sazerac build, and is it ours?
kept.a: The Classic Sazerac at Brennan's is Sazerac rye stirred with Peychaud's bitters, served without ice in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint (ERB-saint), $13; confirm sugar and lemon peel with the bar. The Sazerac Company's own recipe is a sugar cube, three dashes of Peychaud's, an ounce and a half of Sazerac Rye, a quarter ounce of Herbsaint and a lemon peel, built across two glasses and served neat in a chilled rocks glass; the IBA version is Cognac based with absinthe. Give those as the classic, never as the house build. If a guest asks for it on the rocks, check with the bar before promising it. Two luxury versions: Thompson's Dream with Willett rye, and Origin Story with Cognac and absinthe; the price ladder is $13, $20 and $40.

It is strong and served without ice: confirm the glass and the bar's build, sugar and lemon peel included, at lineup. Give the Sazerac Company's recipe only as the classic, never as our house build. Never say America's first cocktail. Say Herbsaint without the H. Pronounce Peychaud's PAY-shoze, and confirm the pharmacy story at lineup before telling it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Brennan’s Irish Coffee
cocktails.serviceNote: Dairy; caffeine; alcohol. On both the breakfast/lunch menu and the dessert menu. Pair with dessert as an upsell.

kept.a: The bar builds the Irish Coffee; you present it. Carry it level so the cream cap stays whole, set it down with the handle toward the guest's right hand, and name it as it lands. Do not stir it: the point is to sip the hot coffee through the cool cream. If the table is having Bananas Foster, bring it just before the flambé, never set down beside the flame. Say: “Here's our Irish Coffee: sip it through the cream, don't stir it.”

Offer the Irish Coffee as dessert arrives, above all with Bananas Foster or the bread pudding, and to a guest lingering after a meal. Next rounds: Ralph's Coffee at $8.00 for a gentler coffee with nut liqueurs, the Espresso Martini at $16.00, or our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory at $11 without whiskey. Say: “With the Foster, our Irish Coffee is lovely: chicory coffee, brown sugar and Tullamore D.E.W. under whipped cream.”

Brennan's Irish Coffee is a signature drink, $12 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: an Irish coffee with a New Orleans accent.

It starts with our dark roast coffee with chicory, CHICK-uh-ree, roasted chicory root blended in the New Orleans way, which adds a roasty, almost chocolatey depth. It is sweetened with brown sugar, spiked with Tullamore D.E.W. Irish whiskey, whose initials are those of Daniel E. Williams, the distillery's manager who became its owner, and topped with whipped cream.

The guest gets a warm coffee under a cool white cap of cream, and sips the hot coffee through it. It tastes warm, sweet and smooth, roasty from the chicory.

It is the dessert upsell, on the breakfast and lunch menu and on the dessert menu: the natural partner for Bananas Foster or the bread pudding. For a guest who wants coffee without whiskey, our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory is the same roast on its own.

Asked: What makes it Brennan's?

Answer: Our dark roast coffee with chicory, the New Orleans tradition, sweetened with brown sugar.

Asked: What whiskey is in it?

Answer: Tullamore D.E.W. Irish whiskey; the initials are those of Daniel E. Williams, the distillery's manager who became its owner.

Asked: Can I have it without alcohol?

Answer: Our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory is the same roast without the whiskey.

It is served hot with a cream cap: carry it level and set it down with the handle toward the guest. It carries caffeine and whiskey. For a guest avoiding alcohol, offer the plain coffee with chicory, which still carries caffeine; for a guest avoiding caffeine, offer the Revive Cold-Pressed Juice, or say “I will ask the bar about decaf.” Fire it with dessert so it arrives with the Foster, not after. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Flamingo

kept.a: In the Roost, offer the Flamingo to anyone celebrating, a couple toasting, or a guest who loves Champagne but wants a cocktail. From the dining room, invite them to the bar: it is poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge. Next rounds in the Roost: the Spoonbill at $36.00 or the Birdcage at $31.00. Say: “For a celebration, the Flamingo is Chopin vodka and Monkey 47 gin with dragonfruit, lemon and Taittinger Champagne.”

The Flamingo is one of the three luxury cocktails poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge, at $28.00, and the Roost's celebration drink.

It pairs Chopin, SHOH-pan, a Polish potato vodka, smooth and round, with Monkey 47, a Black Forest gin bottled at 47 percent with a big botanical lift, then dragonfruit, fresh lemon and Taittinger La Française Champagne, from one of the great Champagne houses. The page prints those five parts; measures, glass and garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a bright, festive glass with fine bubbles. It tastes bright, fruity and dry: citrus and gin botanicals under fine Champagne bubbles, celebratory from the first sip.

It is the drink for an anniversary or a birthday when the guest wants a cocktail rather than a glass of Rare, and a fine reason to start or end the evening in the Roost. Because it is poured only there, a dining room server mentions it as an invitation to the Roost Bar, never as a drink to bring to the table.

Asked: Can I have it at my table in the dining room?

Answer: The Flamingo is poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge; it is a lovely reason to visit the bar before or after dinner.

Asked: Which Champagne is in it?

Answer: Taittinger La Française, from one of the great Champagne houses.

Asked: What is Monkey 47?

Answer: A gin from Germany's Black Forest, bottled at 47 percent, with a big botanical lift.

It is poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge: never promise it at a dining room table. Say Taittinger as teh-tan-ZHAY (TAT-in-jer is often heard) and Chopin as SHOH-pan. Confirm at lineup that it is still on the luxury page, and its measures, glass and garnish. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Birdcage

kept.a: In the Roost, offer the Birdcage to an Old Fashioned or bourbon drinker, and as a nightcap after dinner. From the dining room, invite a whiskey lover to the Roost for it. Next rounds in the Roost: the Spoonbill at $36.00 or the Flamingo at $28.00. Say: “Our Birdcage is a smoked Old Fashioned on Rabbit Hole Dareringer bourbon, with Angostura, orange and cherry: rich, smoky and smooth.”

The Birdcage is one of the three luxury cocktails poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge, at $31.00: our smoked Old Fashioned.

It is built on Rabbit Hole Dareringer, DAIR-ring-er, a Kentucky straight bourbon from Louisville finished in PX sherry casks, so it carries dried fruit and a little extra richness. It is made with Angostura bitters, the classic aromatic bitters of an Old Fashioned, orange and cherry, then smoked, so the first thing the guest meets is the aroma. How the bar smokes it, and the glass and garnish, are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a short, amber drink, wrapped in smoke. It tastes of rich bourbon with dried fruit from the sherry cask, bitters, orange and cherry, under the smoke: rich, smoky and smooth.

It is the Old Fashioned drinker's step up and a slow nightcap for the guest who moves to the Roost after dinner. From the dining room it is an invitation to the bar, never an upsell at the table.

Asked: How is it smoked?

Answer: The page does not say, so I will check with the bar and tell you how they do it tonight.

Asked: What is Dareringer?

Answer: Rabbit Hole Dareringer, a Kentucky straight bourbon from Louisville finished in PX sherry casks, so it carries dried fruit and richness.

Asked: Is it a strong drink?

Answer: It is an Old Fashioned, spirit-forward and made for slow sipping.

It is poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge: never offer it at a dining room table. How it is smoked, the glass and the garnish are lineup questions for the bar. It is spirit-forward: pace a guest who has had several drinks. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Spoonbill

kept.a: In the Roost, offer the Spoonbill to a martini or gin drinker, and at the start of a celebration. From the dining room, a Prisoner of Love drinker is the guest to invite up for it. Next rounds in the Roost: the Flamingo at $28.00 or the Birdcage at $31.00. Say: “The Spoonbill is Hendrick's gin with a Corsican quinquina and chive oil, served with a spoon of caviar.”

The Spoonbill is the grandest of the three luxury cocktails poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge, at $36.00.

It is Hendrick's, HEN-dricks, a Scottish gin with cucumber and rose, with Cap Corse Mattei Blanc, kap KORS mah-TAY, a Corsican quinquina, kan-kee-NAH: a wine aperitif with a gentle bitterness from the same bark that gives tonic water its bite. Chive oil adds a savory, green note, and the drink comes with a spoon of caviar. Which caviar, how much and the glass are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a cool, pale drink and the little spoon of caviar beside it. It tastes of cool cucumber and rose from the gin, a gentle bitter wine note, savory green chive, then the salt of the caviar.

It is a martini drinker's treat, and the caviar makes it a moment, so it suits the start of a celebration. It is poured only in the Roost; from the dining room, it is the grand gin drink to invite a guest up for.

Asked: What is a quinquina?

Answer: Kan-kee-NAH: a wine aperitif with a gentle bitterness, from the same bark that gives tonic water its bite. Ours is Cap Corse Mattei Blanc, from Corsica.

Asked: Which caviar comes with it?

Answer: The page says a spoon of caviar; I will check with the bar which caviar and how much.

Asked: Is it like a martini?

Answer: A savory cousin: gin and an aperitif wine, with chive oil and the caviar alongside.

It is poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge: never offer it at a dining room table. Which caviar, how much, and the glass are lineup questions for the bar; do not describe the caviar until you know. Say Cap Corse Mattei as kap KORS mah-TAY. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Thompson’s Dream

kept.a: Offer Thompson's Dream to a guest ordering a second Sazerac, and to a rye lover who wants more spice. It sits between the Classic at $13 and Origin Story at $40. Next rounds: Origin Story, or Rumors are Flying at $20.00, our barrel-aged rye with tart cherry. Say: “If you loved the Sazerac, Thompson's Dream is the next rung: Willett rye, Creole bitters and a St. George absinthe rinse.”

Thompson's Dream is the middle rung of our Sazerac ladder, $20 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: our Sazerac stepped up.

The guide prints it inside the Classic Sazerac's service note with its build and price. It is Willett 4-year rye, WILL-it, from a family distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, founded in 1936, which runs spicier and stronger than the classic's rye; Bitter Truth Creole Bitters, made in Munich as a tribute to the New Orleans style; and a glass rinsed with St. George absinthe, the first American absinthe made legally after the old ban. No measures, glass or garnish are printed; the build follows the Classic, confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a short, iceless, amber drink like the Classic, with a greener perfume. It tastes of louder rye spice and more heat, with a more herbal rinse.

The name is the house's own; no Willett bottling carries it, so a server says it is probably named for Thompson Willett, the distillery's founder. It is the drink to offer whenever a guest orders a second Sazerac.

Asked: Who is Thompson?

Answer: The name is the house's own. It is probably named for Thompson Willett, who founded the Willett distillery in Bardstown; I would not say more until the bar confirms it.

Asked: How is it different from the Classic Sazerac?

Answer: Willett 4-year rye instead of Sazerac rye, Bitter Truth Creole Bitters instead of Peychaud's, and a St. George absinthe rinse instead of Herbsaint: spicier and bolder.

Asked: What is St. George absinthe?

Answer: A Californian absinthe, the first American one made legally after the old ban.

Say probably named for Thompson Willett, never as a fact, until the bar confirms it. No measures, glass or garnish are printed: confirm them, the Willett bottling and its proof at lineup; the current menu lists it under Sazerac Selections. The Birdcage is a Roost Bar drink, never an upsell at the table. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Next rounds: Thompson's Dream at $20, or the Irish Coffee at $12 to close. Say: “Origin Story is the Sazerac the way it began, on Cognac: Dudognon, barrel-aged Peychaud's and Jade absinthe.”

Origin Story is the top of our Sazerac ladder, $40 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, the highest cocktail price the guide prints.

It is the Sazerac the way it began. The first Sazeracs were Cognac and Peychaud's; rye took over once phylloxera made Cognac scarce in the 1870s and 1880s. So it is built on Dudognon, doo-doh-NYOHN, a family Cognac estate in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first growth, with Peychaud's bitters rested in a barrel and Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe, created by a New Orleans native as a tribute to the city's old absinthe houses. Which Dudognon, and who ages the bitters, are lineup questions.

The guest gets a short, iceless, deep amber drink. It tastes rounder than the Classic: grape, dried fruit and oak, a softer bitters note and a floral wormwood aroma.

It is the drink for the Chateaubriand table, for a guest celebrating, and for the curious drinker who wants to taste where the Sazerac started.

Asked: Why Cognac?

Answer: The first Sazeracs were Cognac and Peychaud's. Rye took over once phylloxera made Cognac scarce in the 1870s and 1880s.

Asked: What is Dudognon?

Answer: Doo-doh-NYOHN: a family Cognac estate in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first growth.

Asked: What makes the bitters barrel-aged?

Answer: The Peychaud's is rested in a barrel. Who ages it and in what cask is a lineup question, so I will check with the bar.

Say the way it began, never the way it was first made. Which Dudognon expression, who barrel-ages the Peychaud's, and the measures are lineup questions; the current menu lists it under Sazerac Selections, misspelled Orgin Story, so say Origin Story. At $40, name the price when you offer it. The Birdcage is a Roost Bar drink, never an upsell at the table. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Brennan’s Bloody Mary

kept.a: Offer the Bloody Mary to a guest who wants a savory eye opener but no beef, and to anyone who orders a Bloody Mary by name. For a guest who wants it richer, the Bloody Bull at $13.00; for a sweeter start, the Brandy Milk Punch at $12.00; without alcohol, the Revive cold-pressed juice at $10.00. Say: “Our Bloody Mary is vodka and our housemade mix with pickled okra and spicy beans: savory, tangy and bright.”

Brennan's Bloody Mary is one of the classic eye openers, $11.00 at breakfast and lunch, the morning drinks New Orleans is known for.

The menu prints four parts: our housemade Bloody Mary mix, vodka, pickled okra and spicy beans. The Bloody Bull's menu line prints a housemade Bloody Mary mix too, with beef bouillon added; whether it is the same batch is a question for the bar, with which vodka, how hot the mix runs today and the glass.

The guest gets a red, savory drink with the pickled okra and spicy beans standing in it. It tastes savory, tangy and spicy, with a pickled crunch.

It is the eye opener for a guest who skips the beef in the Bloody Bull, our other Bloody classic, which is the same idea with beef bouillon stirred in for a richer, meatier drink. For a guest who wants a morning drink without alcohol, the Revive cold-pressed juice takes its place.

Asked: How is it different from the Bloody Bull?

Answer: The Bloody Bull has beef bouillon stirred into its housemade mix; the Bloody Mary does not, and it comes with pickled okra and spicy beans.

Asked: How spicy is it?

Answer: That depends on the mix; I will check with the bar how it is running today.

Asked: Which vodka do you use?

Answer: The menu prints vodka without naming it, so I will check with the bar.

The menu prints the mix as housemade, but not the vodka or the heat: those are lineup questions for the bar. It is the alternative for a guest who skips beef; for any guest asking exactly what is in the mix, the bar answers, not the server. It is poured at breakfast and lunch only. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Brennan’s Champagne Cocktail

kept.a: Present the Champagne Cocktail the moment it leaves the bar, while the bubbles are still rising from the sugar cube: carry it by the stem or the base and set it down at the guest's right. Name it as it lands, and for a celebration toast the occasion in a word. If the bar finishes it at the table, stand back and let the guest watch the fizz climb from the cube. Say: “Here's our Champagne Cocktail: watch the bubbles rise from the sugar. Congratulations.”

Offer the Champagne Cocktail at Bubbles to anyone celebrating, to a couple in the courtyard, and on a Friday before the sabering. For a lighter round, the Riviera at $12.00 or the Chandon Garden Spritz at $15.00; in the Roost, the step up is the Flamingo at $28.00 or the Spoonbill at $36.00. Say: “Our Champagne Cocktail is the classic: Champagne over a sugar cube and Angostura bitters, festive and dry; on Fridays at five, stay for the sabering.”

Brennan's Champagne Cocktail is the house's bubbly classic at Bubbles at Brennan's, $20.00, our afternoon Champagne service in the Roost Bar and the courtyard, where it now sits beside four newer bubbly cocktails.

The menu prints three parts: Champagne, Angostura bitters, ang-guh-STOO-ruh, and a demerara sugar cube. That is the classic build, printed back in 1862: the cube is soaked in bitters, set in the glass, and the Champagne poured over it. Which Champagne, the glass and any garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a glass of Champagne with a steady stream of bubbles rising from the cube. It tastes dry and festive, with a soft spice from the bitters and a faint sweetness as the sugar dissolves.

It is the drink to offer anyone celebrating and a couple in the courtyard, and the grandest of the Bubbles cocktails. Champagne is sabered on Fridays at 5 pm, as the menu prints, and the hours are confirmed on shift.

Answer: Champagne poured over a demerara sugar cube with Angostura bitters, the classic build. Which Champagne we are pouring tonight, I will check with the bar.

The guest gets a sparkling, fruity drink. It tastes of ripe peach and lemon over the gin, with the soft sweetness and fizz of the Bigaro.

It is the drink for a gin lover at Bubbles, and for a guest who likes fruit in a glass of bubbles. A guest who loves it and wants to go grander can follow it with our Champagne Cocktail or, in the Roost, the Spoonbill, our luxury gin drink.

Our New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory is $11 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, priced in the guide's eye openers and coffee list, where one $11 stands before all three coffees.

New Orleans coffee means coffee with chicory. Chicory, CHICK-uh-ree, is a roasted root; the city's habit is usually traced to Civil War blockade shortages, and it stuck because it adds body and a cocoa-like bitterness without any caffeine of its own. The breakfast tasting pours Brennan's private blend from Congregation Coffee, a roaster in Algiers Point, across the river.

The guest gets a hot, dark cup, served the way they take it. It tastes dark, roasty and smooth, with a gentle bitterness.

That bitterness is exactly what balances dessert, which is why the guide makes it the zero-proof pick with six sweet plates: the Framboise French Toast, the coffee cake, Bananas Foster, Cherries Jubilee, the bread pudding and The Snickers. It closes the Traditional Breakfast beside the Foster.

Asked: What is chicory?

Answer: CHICK-uh-ree: a roasted root blended into the coffee, the New Orleans way. It adds body and a cocoa-like bitterness.

Asked: Does chicory have caffeine?

Answer: The chicory itself has none; the coffee does.

Asked: Why chicory in New Orleans?

Answer: The habit is usually traced to wartime shortages in the 1860s, when coffee ran short, and it stuck.

One $11 is printed before all three coffees: confirm at lineup that each is $11, and that the chicory coffee is the Brennan's private blend from Congregation at every meal. On the Traditional Breakfast the coffee with the Foster is included: do not charge it. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Try a sip black first.”

Offer the single origin to a coffee lover, to a guest who wants coffee without chicory, and to anyone asking about local roasters. Read today's origin from the card before you offer it. Next rounds: our New Orleans coffee with chicory, or the Café Glacé de la Maison cold. Say: “If you'd like coffee without chicory, we pour a single origin from Congregation, a roaster just across the river,” then name today's origin from the card.

The Congregation Single-Origin Coffee is $11 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, priced in the guide's eye openers and coffee list beside the chicory coffee.

It is roasted by Congregation Coffee, a roaster in Algiers Point, across the river from the French Quarter. Single origin means the beans come from one place, so the cup tastes of that place rather than a blend, and there is no chicory. The guide printed a Papua New Guinea, but no public listing shows that origin from Congregation, which rotates its single origins with the seasons, so a server reads today's from the coffee card.

The guest gets a hot cup, served the way they take it. It tastes cleaner and brighter than our New Orleans-style coffee; today's tasting notes are on the card.

It is the coffee for the coffee lover who wants no chicory, and a small story about a local roaster to tell at the end of a meal.

cocktails.name: Café Glacé de la Maison

kept.a: The bar builds the Café Glacé; you present it. Carry it level so the orange flower foam stays whole, set it down at the guest's right, and name it as it lands. Suggest the first sip through the foam, so the guest gets the orange flower and the cold coffee together. Say: “Here's our Café Glacé: take the first sip through the foam.”

Offer the Café Glacé to a guest skipping the milk punch, with the baked apple, the turtle soup or the duck confit waffle, and on a warm day. Next rounds: our hot coffee with chicory, or the Personality at $16.00, our spirit-free sparkling rosé drink. Say: “Our Café Glacé de la Maison is chicory cold brew with cardamom and clove, under an orange flower foam: cold, roasty and fragrant.”

The Café Glacé de la Maison is our house iced coffee, $11 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, priced and built in the guide's eye openers and coffee list.

Café glacé, ka-FAY gla-SAY, is French for iced coffee. Ours starts with chicory cold brew, so it is smooth and roasty, sweetened with a syrup of cardamom and clove, the clove a nod to the city's flamed café brûlot, and topped with an orange flower foam.

The guest gets a cold coffee under a pale, fragrant foam. It tastes cold, roasty and lightly sweet, with warm spice and a floral orange lift.

It is the guide's zero-proof pick with the baked apple, the turtle soup and the duck confit waffle, and the cold choice with the coffee cake. It is also the drink for anyone skipping the milk punch at breakfast, and a refreshing, spirit-free choice on a warm courtyard day.

Asked: What is in it?

Answer: Chicory cold brew, a cardamom and clove syrup, and an orange flower foam on top.

Asked: Is there alcohol in it?

Answer: No. It is iced coffee, spirit-free, which makes it the drink for anyone skipping the milk punch.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Lightly: the cardamom and clove syrup sweetens it, and the chicory cold brew keeps it roasty and smooth.

It carries caffeine from the cold brew: offer it with that in mind late in the day. One $11 is printed before all three coffees: confirm each price at lineup. Serve it promptly so the foam holds. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.name: Revive Cold-Pressed Juice

kept.a: Offer the juice to a guest who wants no alcohol and no caffeine, to a light breakfast eater, to a child, and to a guest who turns down the coffee. Next rounds: the Personality at $16.00 or Oh! What It Seemed to Be at $16.00 for something more like a cocktail. Say: “We also pour Revive, a cold-pressed juice of strawberry, apple and pineapple: fresh and bright, with no alcohol.”

Revive Cold-Pressed Juice sits on the breakfast and lunch menu at $10.00, under Cold Pressed Juices, locally made and fresh squeezed, and is used in no pairing.

The menu prints its fruit: strawberry, apple and pineapple. Cold pressing squeezes the fruit without heat, which keeps the juice bright and lively. Who presses it for us, and whether another juice joins it, are questions for the bar.

The guest gets a glass of cold juice. It tastes fresh, sweet and fruity: strawberry first, with apple and the tang of pineapple.

It is the drink for a guest who wants neither alcohol nor caffeine, and for anyone who would like something light with breakfast. It suits a child or a guest who is not drinking and does not want coffee, and it gives a breakfast table a fresh option beside the eye openers.

Asked: What flavor is it?

Answer: Strawberry, apple and pineapple, as the menu prints it, pressed locally and served cold.

Asked: What does cold-pressed mean?

Answer: The fruit is squeezed without heat, which keeps the juice bright and lively.

Asked: Is there caffeine in it?

Answer: No, and no alcohol: it is simply cold-pressed fruit juice, a fresh start to breakfast and a good choice for a child at the table.

The menu prints one juice, Revive, with strawberry, apple and pineapple: name those, and ask the bar before promising any other. cocktails.name: For Sentimental Reasons

kept.a: Offer For Sentimental Reasons at the start of brunch or dinner, to a table celebrating, and to a guest who would otherwise order a glass of sparkling wine. Next rounds: To Each His Own at $18.00 for orchard fruit with more depth, the Prisoner of Love at $16.00 for a gin drink, or the Personality at $16.00 without alcohol. Say: “For Sentimental Reasons is pear and warm allspice topped with sparkling wine: fizzy, fruity and a lovely way to start.”

For Sentimental Reasons is the first drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $15.00, the lowest price on that list. The list celebrates 80 years of Brennan's, which opened in 1946, and each drink carries the title of a song from that year.

The menu prints three parts: allspice dram, a liqueur that tastes of warm baking spice, then pear purée, topped with sparkling wine. Which sparkling wine, which allspice dram, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a sparkling drink with the soft body the purée gives. It tastes fizzy and fruity, ripe pear first, with a gentle spice on the finish.

It is the lightest way into the fall list: a brunch drink, a toast for a celebration, and the one to offer a guest who usually orders a glass of bubbles. Its spirit-free neighbor on the menu is the Personality, a sparkling rosé drink.

Asked: What is allspice dram?

Answer: A liqueur flavored with allspice, the berry that tastes like clove, cinnamon and nutmeg together. Which one our bar pours, I will check with the bar.

Asked: Why are the drinks named for songs?

Answer: The fall list is Billboard Songs from 1946, the year Brennan's opened, for our 80 years. Each drink carries the title of a song from that year.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Fruity rather than sugary: the pear gives softness and the bubbles keep it bright.

Say the full name, For Sentimental Reasons, when you ring it, so the bar never has to guess between song titles. Which sparkling wine, which allspice dram, the measures, the glass and the garnish are lineup questions for the bar; describe only the three printed parts until then. It is a sparkling drink: carry it straight from the bar so it keeps its fizz. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

cocktails.serviceNote: Clarified heavy cream, as printed. Alcohol. Confirm at lineup before you answer a guest's question about cream.

kept.a: Offer the Prisoner of Love to a gin drinker, to a tea lover, and to a guest who wants something silky and fragrant before dinner or as a gentle nightcap. Next rounds: Five Minutes More at $20.00 for a bolder herbal drink, For Sentimental Reasons at $15.00 for bubbles, or the Personality at $16.00 without alcohol. Say: “Prisoner of Love is gin with Earl Grey tea and orange flower water, made silky with clarified cream.”

Prisoner of Love is the gin drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $16.00. Like every drink on the list, it carries the title of a song from 1946, the year Brennan's opened.

The menu prints gin, Earl Grey tea, clarified heavy cream and orange flower water. Clarifying is the old milk punch technique, where the milk is curdled and strained off clear; it leaves a silky texture without the weight of cream. Which gin, how our bar clarifies the cream, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a fragrant, silky drink. It tastes of the bergamot in the tea and a floral orange note over the gin.

It is the drink for a gin lover who wants something gentler than a martini, and a good talking point for anyone curious about cocktail history: milk punch is an old New Orleans habit, and our Brandy Milk Punch, the cold, creamy kind, opens the Traditional Breakfast.

Asked: What is clarified heavy cream?

Answer: Cream used the old milk punch way: it is curdled and strained off clear, so the drink keeps a silky texture without being heavy. How our bar does it, I will check with the bar.

Asked: Is it creamy like a milk punch?

Answer: The menu prints clarified heavy cream: in the old method the solids are strained out, so it drinks smooth rather than thick. How our bar makes it, I will check with the bar.

Asked: Which gin is it?

Answer: The menu does not name it; I will check with the bar.

Do not describe it as a cream drink: the cream is clarified, and a guest expecting a milk punch may be surprised. Do not confuse it with the Brandy Milk Punch, our breakfast eye opener. Which gin, how the cream is clarified, the measures, the glass and the garnish are lineup questions for the bar. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.
