cocktails.name: Rumors are Flying

kept.a: Offer Rumors are Flying to a guest who orders an Old Fashioned, to a rye lover, and as a slow drink after dinner. Next rounds: the Classic Sazerac at $13.00 to try the New Orleans original, Thompson's Dream at $20.00 for more spice, or the Personality at $16.00, its spirit-free twin. Say: “Rumors are Flying is our own barrel-aged Rittenhouse rye with tart cherry and brown sugar: rich, spicy and a little tart.”

Rumors are Flying is the whiskey drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $20.00, the top price on the list beside Five Minutes More.

The menu prints Brennan's Barrel Aged Rittenhouse Rye, then tart cherry juice, brown sugar syrup and orange bitters. The rye carries the Brennan's name and a barrel: who aged it, in what cask and for how long are questions for the bar, so a server says barrel-aged for Brennan's and no more. The measures, the method, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar too.

The guest gets a dark, spirit-forward drink. It tastes rich: rye spice and oak, with dark tart cherry and a warm brown sugar roundness.

It is the drink for an Old Fashioned lover, and the bridge to our Sazerac ladder. Its spirit-free twin on the menu is the Personality, which shares the tart cherry juice and brown sugar syrup.

Asked: What is Brennan's barrel-aged rye?

Answer: Rittenhouse rye aged in a barrel under the Brennan's name. Who aged it and for how long, I will check with the bar.

Asked: Is it like an Old Fashioned?

Answer: Close: rye, sugar and bitters, with tart cherry juice for brightness.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Rich rather than sweet: the brown sugar rounds the rye and the tart cherry keeps it bright.

Do not mix it up with the Personality, its spirit-free twin: both carry tart cherry juice and brown sugar syrup, so repeat the name when you ring it. Say barrel-aged for Brennan's and no more until the bar tells you who aged the rye and for how long. The measures, the glass and whether it comes over ice are lineup questions. cocktails.name: To Each His Own

kept.a: Offer To Each His Own to a brandy or Cognac drinker, to a guest who loves apple desserts, and as a fall aperitif before dinner. Next rounds: Origin Story at $40.00 for the Sazerac on Cognac, For Sentimental Reasons at $15.00 for something sparkling, or the Apple Crumble at $15.00 with dessert. Say: “To Each His Own is Calvados, an apple brandy, with Lillet Blanc and quince: fall orchard fruit in a glass.”

To Each His Own is the orchard drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $18.00, named like the others for a song of the year Brennan's opened.

The menu prints three parts. Daron Fine Calvados, dah-ROHN KAL-vuh-dohs, is apple brandy from northern France; Fine is the youngest grade of Calvados, fresh and fruity. Lillet Blanc, lee-LAY BLAHN, is a light French aperitif wine, floral and citrusy. The quince liqueur brings a fruit between an apple and a pear, very fragrant. Which quince liqueur, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a smooth, spirit-forward drink. It tastes of baked apple and perfumed quince, softened and lifted by the Lillet.

It is the drink for a brandy lover, and the most seasonal flavor on the fall list. For the next brandy round, our Origin Story is the Sazerac on Cognac.

Asked: What is Calvados?

Answer: KAL-vuh-dohs: apple brandy from northern France. Ours is Daron Fine.

Asked: What is quince?

Answer: A fragrant fruit somewhere between an apple and a pear, often cooked into preserves. Which quince liqueur we pour, I will check with the bar.

Asked: Is it strong?

Answer: It is spirit-forward, brandy with an aperitif wine and a liqueur, so it is a drink to sip slowly.

Say Calvados, not Cognac: both are French brandy, but Calvados is apple brandy. The same Lillet Blanc goes into the Riviera at Bubbles, so name the drink clearly when you ring it. Which quince liqueur, the measures, the glass and the garnish are lineup questions for the bar. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Old Buttermilk Sky is the tequila sour on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $18.00, named for one of the songs of the year Brennan's opened.

The menu prints Volcán Reposado Tequila, vol-KAHN reh-poh-SAH-doh, a tequila rested in oak, rounder than an unaged one; then fig liqueur, lemon, cinnamon syrup and egg white. Egg white is the classic way to give a sour its silky body. Which fig liqueur, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a sour with a silky texture. It tastes warm and fruity, ripe fig and cinnamon over the rested tequila, with lemon keeping it bright.

It is the drink for a margarita or whiskey sour lover who wants something for fall. Its spirit-free twin on the menu, Oh! What It Seemed to Be, follows the same pattern on Lyre's non-alcoholic agave spirit with fig syrup, so a table can share the idea whether or not they drink.

kept.a: Offer Five Minutes More to a guest who asks for something herbal, to a vodka drinker who wants more flavor, and to an adventurous table. Next rounds: Old Buttermilk Sky at $18.00 for a silky sour, the Prisoner of Love at $16.00 for a gentler gin drink, or the Espresso Martini at $16.00 after dinner. Say: “Five Minutes More is mandarin vodka with Green Chartreuse, Licor 43 and lemon: bright, herbal and a little sweet.”

Five Minutes More is the herbal drink on our fall list, Billboard Songs from 1946, at $20.00, the top price on the list beside Rumors are Flying. Its name is the title of a song from 1946, the year Brennan's opened.

The menu prints four parts: Cathead Mandarin Vodka, a mandarin flavored vodka; Green Chartreuse, shar-TROOZ, a French herbal liqueur, intense and green; Licor 43, lee-KOR kwah-REN-tah ee TRESS, a Spanish liqueur with vanilla and citrus; and lemon. The measures, the method, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a bright, citrusy drink. It tastes of mandarin and lemon first, then the deep green herbs of the Chartreuse, with a soft vanilla sweetness from the Licor 43 on the finish.

It is the drink for a guest who loves herbal liqueurs, and for a vodka drinker who wants more character than a vodka soda. It is strong and layered, so it sips slowly.

Asked: What is Green Chartreuse?

Answer: Shar-TROOZ: a French herbal liqueur, green, intense and high in alcohol.

Asked: What is Licor 43?

Answer: Lee-KOR kwah-REN-tah ee TRESS: a Spanish liqueur that tastes of vanilla and citrus.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Balanced: the lemon keeps it bright and the liqueurs give it a gentle sweetness. If you prefer it drier, I will ask the bar.

Name both liqueurs clearly: Green Chartreuse and Licor 43 are the talking points, and the Chartreuse is high in alcohol, so let the guest know it is a strong drink. The measures, the glass and the garnish are lineup questions for the bar. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Say: “Personality is a zero proof sparkling rosé with tart cherry and brown sugar: festive, fizzy and spirit-free.”

Personality is one of the two spirit-free drinks on our current menu, under Temperance, 1946, at $16.00. Like the Billboard Songs from 1946 cocktails beside it, it carries the title of a song from the year Brennan's opened.

The guest gets a pink, sparkling drink. It tastes fizzy and bright, red fruit and tart cherry, with a gentle warmth from the brown sugar.

It is the drink that lets a guest who is not drinking join the toast, at brunch or at a birthday. It shares its tart cherry juice and brown sugar syrup with Rumors are Flying, the rye drink on the fall list, so a couple can order the same idea with and without spirit.

Floating in South Africa opens our three dessert cocktails, on the dessert menu at $15.00: a root beer float for grown-ups.

The vanilla bean ice cream is made in house, and Abita root beer comes from Abita Springs, Louisiana, the brewery behind the Abita Amber in our Shells & Cheese. The measures, the glass and how it is built are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a creamy, fizzy drink with ice cream in it. It tastes sweet and nostalgic: vanilla, root beer spice and the rich caramel note of the Amarula.

It is the playful close to a meal, dessert and drink in one, and a natural for a birthday table or anyone who grew up on floats.

Asked: What is Amarula?

Answer: Am-uh-ROO-luh: a South African cream liqueur made with the fruit of the marula tree, rich and caramel-like.

Say: “Banane au Chocolat is banana and chocolate liqueurs with Pedro Ximénez sherry: rich, silky and sweet, the Foster you can sip.”

Banane au Chocolat, bah-NAHN oh shoh-koh-LAH, is the banana and chocolate drink among our three dessert cocktails, at $16.00, the top price of the three. The name is French for banana with chocolate.

The menu prints three parts: crème de banana and crème de cocoa, two classic dessert liqueurs, and Pedro Ximénez sherry, PAY-droh hee-MEH-nez, the sweetest style of sherry, dark and syrupy, tasting of raisins and figs. Which liqueurs, which sherry, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a dark, silky dessert drink. It tastes of ripe banana and chocolate, with the sherry's dried fruit depth underneath.

It is the drink for a chocolate lover and a fine companion to the house's banana story: Bananas Foster was invented at Brennan's in 1951. A guest who loves the Foster but cannot manage another dessert can sip this instead.

Asked: What is Pedro Ximénez?

Answer: PAY-droh hee-MEH-nez: the sweetest style of Spanish sherry, dark and syrupy, made from the grape of the same name.

Asked: Is it very sweet?

Answer: Yes, it is a true dessert drink, rich and silky; a coffee alongside balances it well.

Asked: Does it taste like Bananas Foster?

Answer: It shares the banana and the richness, with chocolate and sherry in place of the rum and butter.

Say it bah-NAHN oh shoh-koh-LAH, and do not mix it up with Floating in South Africa, the dessert drink with ice cream: this one has none. Which liqueurs and which sherry, the measures and the glass are lineup questions for the bar. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

So it's rich and silky, ripe banana and chocolate with a dark, dried fruit depth. Here, where Bananas Foster was invented, it's the banana dessert you can sip. It's $16.00, the top of our dessert cocktails.

cocktails.name: Espresso Martini
cocktails.serviceNote: Chicory, Frangelico, a hazelnut liqueur, and Kahlua, as printed. Alcohol. Confirm at lineup before you answer a guest's question about nuts or caffeine.

kept.a: Offer the Espresso Martini as dessert menus go down, to a vodka drinker, and to a table that wants coffee and a nightcap at once. Next rounds: Ralph's Coffee at $8.00 for something gentler, Brennan's Irish Coffee at $12.00, or the Banane au Chocolat at $16.00 for chocolate. Say: “Our Espresso Martini has a New Orleans accent: vodka with chicory, Frangelico and Kahlua, roasty and smooth.”

Our Espresso Martini is the first of the two coffee cocktails on the dessert menu, at $16.00: the modern classic with a New Orleans accent.

The menu prints chicory, vodka, Frangelico and Kahlua. Chicory, CHICK-uh-ree, is the roasted root New Orleans blends into its coffee, which adds body and a cocoa-like bitterness. Frangelico, fran-JEL-ih-koh, is an Italian hazelnut liqueur, and Kahlua, kuh-LOO-uh, a coffee liqueur. Whether the chicory comes as our chicory coffee or another way, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a dark coffee cocktail. It tastes roasty and smooth: chicory and coffee liqueur, toasted hazelnut, and clean vodka underneath.

It is the drink for a guest who wants dessert and a coffee in one glass, and for a vodka drinker at the end of a meal. Ralph's Coffee, beside it on the menu, carries the Frangelico too, in coffee under whipped cream.

Asked: Is there espresso in it?

Answer: The menu prints chicory with the vodka, Frangelico and Kahlua; I will check with the bar whether it is made with our chicory coffee or espresso.

Asked: Will it keep me awake?

Answer: That depends on the coffee in it, so I will check with the bar. Chicory itself carries no caffeine.

Asked: What is Frangelico?

Answer: Fran-JEL-ih-koh: an Italian hazelnut liqueur.

Do not promise caffeine or no caffeine: chicory carries none, and the bar knows what else is in the glass. The menu calls it an Espresso Martini but prints chicory, so confirm the coffee at lineup. Frangelico is a hazelnut liqueur: read the service note and confirm at lineup before answering ingredient questions. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

The build is the menu's own; measures and glass are not printed: confirm with the bar. The menu prints chicory, not espresso: confirm the coffee with the bar.

So it's roasty and smooth, coffee and toasted hazelnut over clean vodka. It's the drink for a guest who wants dessert and a nightcap at once, and a fine partner for Bananas Foster or the bread pudding. It's $16.00.

cocktails.name: Ralph’s Coffee
cocktails.serviceNote: Frangelico and Nocello, the two nut liqueurs, and whipped cream, as printed, over hot coffee with chicory. Alcohol. Confirm at lineup before you answer a guest's question about nuts, cream or caffeine.

kept.a: The bar builds Ralph's Coffee and you present it. Carry it level so the cream cap stays whole, turn any handle toward the guest's right hand, and say the name as you set it down so it is never taken for the Irish Coffee. Ask the guest not to stir: the coffee is meant to be sipped through the cream. At a Bananas Foster table, bring it just before the flame, never beside it. Say: “Here's Ralph's Coffee: hazelnut and walnut in our chicory coffee. Sip it through the cream.”

Offer Ralph's Coffee as dessert arrives, with Bananas Foster or the bread pudding, and to a guest who wants a coffee with a little something but not a whiskey drink. Next rounds: Brennan's Irish Coffee at $12.00 with whiskey, the Espresso Martini at $16.00, or our New Orleans Style Coffee at $11.00 on its own. Say: “Ralph's Coffee is our chicory coffee with hazelnut and walnut liqueurs under whipped cream: nutty and comforting.”

Ralph's Coffee is the second coffee cocktail on our dessert menu, at $8.00, the lowest cocktail price on the menu.

The menu prints dark roast coffee with chicory, CHICK-uh-ree, the same coffee that goes into Brennan's Irish Coffee, then Frangelico, fran-JEL-ih-koh, an Italian hazelnut liqueur, and Nocello, noh-CHEL-oh, an Italian walnut liqueur, under whipped cream. The measures and the glass are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a coffee under a white cap of cream, and sips the coffee through it. It tastes roasty and nutty, hazelnut and walnut in the chicory coffee, with the cool cream on top.

It is the gentle choice beside the Irish Coffee: no whiskey and no brown sugar, the nut liqueurs instead. The menu does not say who it is named for, so a server tells no story about the name until a manager gives one. With Bananas Foster or the bread pudding, it is the easiest way to keep a table lingering.

Asked: Who is Ralph?

Answer: The menu does not say; I will check with a manager before I tell you a story about the name.

Asked: How is it different from the Irish Coffee?

Answer: Same chicory coffee and whipped cream, but with hazelnut and walnut liqueurs in place of Irish whiskey and brown sugar.

Asked: What is Nocello?

Answer: Noh-CHEL-oh: an Italian walnut liqueur.

Do not mix it up with Brennan's Irish Coffee: both are chicory coffee under whipped cream, so name the drink as you ring it and as it lands. Confirm at lineup that it is served hot, and in which glass. It carries two nut liqueurs and cream: read the service note and confirm at lineup before answering ingredient questions. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.
